name: Earth & Space
tagline: The planet beneath us and the cosmos above.

nodes.title: Day and Night
nodes.goal: Sun, moon and stars across the day.

lesson_media.alt: A brass lamp lights one half of a globe; a small house stands near the boundary between light and dark, and an arrow circles the globe.
lesson_media.caption: Earth's rotation carries one place into sunlight and then into darkness. The Moon can appear by day or night, and stars remain in the daytime sky even when scattered sunlight hides most of them.

lesson_media.title: Turn through one day
lesson_media.instructions: Advance six hours at a time through a simplified equinox day at the equator. Follow one place as Earth's rotation carries it through sunrise, midday, sunset and midnight.

nodes.kid_text: Earth turns once each day. The side facing the Sun has daylight. As your place turns away from the Sun, the sky grows dark; as it turns back, morning begins. The Moon can be visible in daytime or at night. Stars are still beyond the daytime sky too, but bright scattered sunlight hides most of them from our eyes.

quiz.prompt: Which can often be seen in a clear night sky? 🌃
choices: Moon 🌙
Sun ☀️
Rainbow 🌈
quiz.answer: Moon 🌙
quiz.say: Which can often be seen in a clear night sky — the moon, the sun, or a rainbow?
quiz.explain: The Moon is often visible at night because it reflects sunlight. It can also be visible during part of the day.

quiz.prompt: Dark sky, twinkly stars. ⭐ When?
choices: Night 🌙
Day ☀️
Morning 🌅
quiz.answer: Night 🌙
quiz.say: The sky is dark and full of twinkly stars. Is it night 🌙, day ☀️, or morning 🌅?
quiz.explain: A dark sky makes many stars easier to see, so this scene is at night. The stars are still there during the day.

quiz.prompt: What makes the day warm and bright?
choices: Sun ☀️
Moon 🌙
Stars ⭐
quiz.answer: Sun ☀️
quiz.say: In the day time, what shines bright and keeps us warm? The sun ☀️, the moon 🌙, or the stars ⭐?
quiz.explain: Sunlight makes daytime bright and warms Earth's surface.

quiz.prompt: Tiny twinkly lights up high?
choices: Stars ⭐
Clouds ☁️
Snow ❄️
quiz.answer: Stars ⭐
quiz.say: At night you can see tiny lights twinkling way up high. Are they stars ⭐, clouds ☁️, or snow ❄️?
quiz.explain: Stars are distant suns. Their light can seem to twinkle as it passes through Earth's moving atmosphere.

quiz.prompt: Morning time! What comes up? 🐓
choices: Sun ☀️
Moon 🌙
Stars ⭐
quiz.answer: Sun ☀️
quiz.say: It is morning and the sky is getting bright. What is coming up? The sun ☀️, the moon 🌙, or the stars ⭐?
quiz.explain: The Sun appears to rise as Earth's rotation turns your place toward it.

quiz.prompt: Why are most stars hard to see in daytime? ☀️⭐
choices: Scattered sunlight hides their light
The stars switch off during the day
The stars leave the sky each morning
quiz.answer: Scattered sunlight hides their light
quiz.say: Why are most stars hard to see in daytime? Does bright scattered sunlight hide their faint light, do the stars switch off, or do they leave the sky?
quiz.explain: The stars remain in the sky, but sunlight scattered through the atmosphere makes the sky bright and hides most of their light from our eyes.

quiz.prompt: The sun goes down. Then comes…?
choices: Night 🌙
Morning 🌅
Noon 🕛
quiz.answer: Night 🌙
quiz.say: When the sun goes down and the sky gets dark, what comes next? Night 🌙, morning 🌅, or noon 🕛?
quiz.explain: As Earth rotates, your place turns away from the Sun and night begins. The Moon or stars may be visible when they are above the horizon and the sky is clear.

nodes.title: Weather
nodes.goal: Rain, sun, wind and snow.
nodes.kid_text: Weather is what the sky is doing outside today. Sometimes rain falls in wet drops, sometimes the Sun makes everything warm, sometimes the wind pushes the leaves, and sometimes cold snow floats down like white feathers. Look out the window and you can see the weather!

quiz.prompt: Drops fall from a cloud. 🪟 What is it?
choices: Rain 💧
Snow ❄️
Wind 🍃
quiz.answer: Rain 💧
quiz.say: Little wet drops are falling down from a cloud. Is it rain 💧, snow ❄️, or wind 🍃?
quiz.explain: Rain is little drops of water falling from a cloud.

quiz.prompt: Cold and white, floats down soft?
choices: Snow ❄️
Rain 💧
Sun ☀️
quiz.answer: Snow ❄️
quiz.say: Which weather is cold and white and floats down softly like feathers? Snow ❄️, rain 💧, or sun ☀️?
quiz.explain: Snow is cold and white, and it floats down very softly.

quiz.prompt: What pushes the leaves around? 🌳
choices: Wind 🍃
Rain 💧
Snow ❄️
quiz.answer: Wind 🍃
quiz.say: The leaves on the tree are moving. What pushes them around? Wind, rain, or snow?
quiz.explain: Wind is moving air, and it pushes leaves all around.

quiz.prompt: Which weather makes your coat wet?
choices: Rain 💧
Wind 🍃
Sun ☀️
quiz.answer: Rain 💧
quiz.say: Which weather would make your coat all wet outside? Rain 💧, wind 🍃, or sun ☀️?
quiz.explain: Rain is drops of water, so it makes everything wet.

quiz.prompt: Need mittens and a warm hat for…? 🧤
choices: Snow ❄️
Sun ☀️
Wind 🍃
quiz.answer: Snow ❄️
quiz.say: When do you most need warm mittens and a woolly hat? In snow ❄️, in sun ☀️, or in wind 🍃?
quiz.explain: Snow is the coldest of these, so we wrap up warm.

quiz.prompt: What lifts a kite up high? 🪁
choices: Wind 🍃
Rain 💧
Snow ❄️
quiz.answer: Wind 🍃
quiz.say: Something lifts your kite way up into the sky. Is it wind 🍃, rain 💧, or snow ❄️?
quiz.explain: Wind is moving air, and it can lift a kite up high.

quiz.prompt: Which weather warms your face?
choices: Sun ☀️
Wind 🍃
Snow ❄️
quiz.answer: Sun ☀️
quiz.say: Which weather feels warm and cosy on your face? Sun ☀️, wind 🍃, or snow ❄️?
quiz.explain: The sun shines down and makes us feel warm.

lesson_media.alt: A weather cycle links uneven solar heating to evaporation, rising and cooling air, cloud condensation, and rain or snow returning water.
lesson_media.caption: Weather is not produced by clouds alone: moving energy, water, and air pressure create the changing conditions we observe.

nodes.title: Land and Water
nodes.goal: Mountains, rivers and seas.
nodes.kid_text: Some land is flat and some pokes up high into tall mountains you can climb. Water runs along the ground in wiggly rivers, and it gathers into the huge blue sea where waves splash. Earth has both dry land and lots of water!

quiz.prompt: Which one pokes up very high?
choices: Mountain 🏔️
Sea 🌊
River 💧
quiz.answer: Mountain 🏔️
quiz.say: Which one pokes up high into the sky? A mountain 🏔️, the sea 🌊, or a river 💧?
quiz.explain: A mountain is land that goes way, way up high.

quiz.prompt: Where do big waves splash? 🏖️
choices: Sea 🌊
Hill 🌄
Rock 🪨
quiz.answer: Sea 🌊
quiz.say: You are standing on the sand. Where do the big waves splash? The sea, a hill, or a rock?
quiz.explain: Waves splash in the big blue sea.

quiz.prompt: Which one is made of water?
choices: River 💧
Rock 🪨
Hill 🌄
quiz.answer: River 💧
quiz.say: Which one is made of water running along the ground? A river 💧, a rock 🪨, or a hill 🌄?
quiz.explain: A river is water wiggling along the ground.

quiz.prompt: Which one can you climb up? 🥾
choices: Mountain 🏔️
River 💧
Sea 🌊
quiz.answer: Mountain 🏔️
quiz.say: Which one can you climb up with your boots on? A mountain 🏔️, a river 💧, or the sea 🌊?
quiz.explain: A mountain is tall land, so you can climb it.

quiz.prompt: A boat floats on…? ⛵
choices: Water 💧
Sand 🏖️
Grass 🌱
quiz.answer: Water 💧
quiz.say: A little boat floats along. Does it float on water 💧, on sand 🏖️, or on grass 🌱?
quiz.explain: Boats float on water, like on a river or the sea.

quiz.prompt: Wiggly water on the land is a…?
choices: River 💧
Hill 🌄
Cloud ☁️
quiz.answer: River 💧
quiz.say: Water wiggles along the ground like a long ribbon. Is that a river 💧, a hill 🌄, or a cloud ☁️?
quiz.explain: A river is water that wiggles along the land.

quiz.prompt: Which one holds the most water?
choices: Sea 🌊
Puddle 💦
Cup 🥤
quiz.answer: Sea 🌊
quiz.say: Which one holds the most water? The sea 🌊, a puddle 💦, or a cup 🥤?
quiz.explain: The sea is huge, much bigger than a puddle or a cup.

lesson_media.alt: A watershed diagram routes rain and snow from a mountain through streams, groundwater, river, delta, and ocean while tracking erosion and deposition.
lesson_media.caption: Gravity connects landforms and water: drainage pathways both follow the landscape and gradually reshape it.

nodes.title: Why Seasons Happen
nodes.goal: The tilted, orbiting Earth.

lesson_media.alt: Four views of a tilted Earth orbit the Sun, with budding, leafy, autumn-colored and bare branches nearby.
lesson_media.caption: This schematic is not to scale. Earth's axis keeps nearly the same direction as Earth orbits, changing sunlight angle and day length; opposite hemispheres have opposite seasons, and not every region uses four temperate-season labels.

lesson_media.title: Compare tilt through the year
lesson_media.instructions: Choose one of four orbital positions and either hemisphere. Compare daylight and sunlight angle in this not-to-scale model; axial tilt, not Earth's small distance changes, drives the seasonal pattern.

nodes.kid_text: Earth's axis is tilted and keeps pointing nearly the same way as Earth travels around the Sun. When the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, it gets longer days and more direct sunlight, while the Southern Hemisphere gets shorter days and more slanted sunlight. About half a year later, the pattern reverses. Tilt, not Earth's small changes in distance from the Sun, causes this cycle. Temperate places often name four seasons. Tropical and polar regions, and many cultural calendars, may describe seasonal changes differently.

quiz.prompt: 🌍 travels around what?
choices: The Sun
The Moon
The stars
quiz.answer: The Sun
quiz.say: Earth travels in one big loop all year long. What does it travel around? The Sun, the Moon, or the stars?
quiz.explain: Earth travels in a big loop all the way around the Sun.

quiz.prompt: At the June solstice, the Northern Hemisphere has…?
choices: Summer
Winter
Autumn
quiz.answer: Summer
quiz.say: At the June solstice, the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun. Does it have summer, winter, or autumn?
quiz.explain: The Northern Hemisphere has summer around the June solstice, with longer days and more direct sunlight. The Southern Hemisphere has winter then.

quiz.prompt: One trip around the Sun takes…?
choices: A year
A day
A month
quiz.answer: A year
quiz.say: How long does Earth take to go all the way around the Sun? A year, a day, or a month?
quiz.explain: Earth takes one whole year to go all the way around.

quiz.prompt: In a temperate winter, sunlight arrives…?
choices: More slanted and spread out
More direct and concentrated
Just the same as summer
quiz.answer: More slanted and spread out
quiz.say: In a temperate winter, how does sunlight arrive — more slanted and spread out, more direct and concentrated, or just the same as summer?
quiz.explain: More slanted sunlight spreads the same incoming energy over a larger area, and shorter days provide less time for heating.

quiz.prompt: Northern summer means the Southern Hemisphere has…?
choices: Winter
Summer
Spring
quiz.answer: Winter
quiz.say: When the Northern Hemisphere has summer, does the Southern Hemisphere have winter, summer, or spring?
quiz.explain: The hemispheres have opposite astronomical seasons: Southern winter occurs during Northern summer.

quiz.prompt: What mainly changes seasonal sunlight?
choices: Earth's tilt
Earth moving nearer the Sun
The Sun getting hotter
quiz.answer: Earth's tilt
quiz.say: What mainly changes seasonal sunlight — Earth's tilt, Earth moving nearer the Sun, or the Sun getting hotter?
quiz.explain: Earth's tilt changes day length and sunlight angle. Earth's orbit is slightly elliptical, but its distance changes are not the cause of opposite seasons in the two hemispheres.

quiz.prompt: A temperate four-season calendar names how many seasons?
quiz.say: In a temperate four-season calendar, how many seasons are named — 4, 2, or 12?
quiz.explain: That calendar names spring, summer, autumn and winter. Other regions and cultures may describe the year's seasonal cycle differently.

nodes.title: The Solar System
nodes.goal: The Sun, eight planets and their moons.
nodes.kid_text: Our Sun is a giant glowing star, and eight planets travel around it in big loops. Earth is one of those planets, and we live on it! Some planets also have their own moons circling them, just like our Moon circles Earth.

quiz.prompt: How many planets go around our Sun? 🪐
quiz.say: How many planets travel around our Sun? Is it 8, 9, or 4?
quiz.explain: There are eight planets looping around our Sun, and Earth is one of them.

quiz.prompt: Our Sun is a big…?
choices: Star
Planet
Moon
quiz.answer: Star
quiz.say: Our Sun is a giant glowing ball of light. Is it a star, a planet, or a moon?
quiz.explain: The Sun is a star, and it is the closest star to us.

quiz.prompt: What circles around Earth? 🌍
choices: The Moon
The Sun
Mars
quiz.answer: The Moon
quiz.say: Something goes around and around our Earth. Is it the Moon, the Sun, or Mars?
quiz.explain: The Moon circles Earth, while Earth circles the Sun.

quiz.prompt: Which one do we live on?
choices: Earth
Mars
The Moon
quiz.answer: Earth
quiz.say: Which one is our home, the place we live? Earth, Mars, or the Moon?
quiz.explain: We live on Earth, one of the eight planets.

quiz.prompt: What sits in the middle? 🪐
choices: The Sun
Earth
The Moon
quiz.answer: The Sun
quiz.say: The planets all loop around one thing in the middle. Is it the Sun, Earth, or the Moon?
quiz.explain: The Sun sits in the middle, and every planet loops around it.

quiz.prompt: Do other planets have moons too?
choices: Yes
No
quiz.answer: Yes
quiz.say: Earth has one moon. Do other planets have moons of their own? Yes, or no?
quiz.explain: Yes! Most planets have moons, and some have dozens.

quiz.prompt: Planets travel around the Sun in big…?
choices: Loops
Straight lines
Zigzags
quiz.answer: Loops
quiz.say: How do the planets travel around the Sun? In big loops, in straight lines, or in zigzags?
quiz.explain: Planets go around the Sun in big round loops.

lesson_media.alt: An ordered Solar System line names Mercury through Neptune and distinguishes four rocky planets, two gas giants, and two ice giants.
lesson_media.caption: The sequence is reliable while the compressed drawing is not distance or size scale—a crucial distinction when reading Solar System diagrams.

nodes.title: Rocks and Soil
nodes.goal: Kinds of rock; how soil forms.
nodes.kid_text: Rocks come in many kinds: some are smooth, some are rough, some sparkle, and some have stripes. When rocks get bumped and broken into teeny tiny bits over a very long time, and mix with bits of old leaves, they make soil. Plants push their roots into soil to grow, so soil comes from broken rocks!

quiz.prompt: Soil is made from broken…?
choices: Rocks
Seeds
Water
quiz.answer: Rocks
quiz.say: Tiny broken bits mix with old leaves to make soil. Broken bits of what? Rocks, seeds, or water?
quiz.explain: Soil is tiny broken rock mixed with bits of old leaves.

quiz.prompt: Where do plant roots grow best? 🌱
choices: Soil
Solid rock
Air
quiz.answer: Soil
quiz.say: Where does a plant push its roots down to grow best? Into soil, into solid rock, or into air?
quiz.explain: Roots push into soft soil, where there is water and food.

quiz.prompt: Hot melted rock from a volcano is…? 🌋
choices: Lava
Sand
Soil
quiz.answer: Lava
quiz.say: A volcano pours out rock so hot that it runs like syrup. Is that lava, sand, or soil?
quiz.explain: Lava is melted rock, and it turns hard and stony when it cools.

quiz.prompt: Which animal mixes up the soil?
choices: Worm 🪱
Fish 🐟
Bee 🐝
quiz.answer: Worm 🪱
quiz.say: Which animal tunnels through the ground and mixes up the soil? A worm 🪱, a fish 🐟, or a bee 🐝?
quiz.explain: Worms tunnel through soil, mixing it up and letting air in.

quiz.prompt: Are all rocks the same? 🪨
choices: No
Yes
quiz.answer: No
quiz.say: Some rocks sparkle, some have stripes, some are rough. Are all rocks the same? No, or yes?
quiz.explain: Rocks come in many kinds, so they are not all the same.

quiz.prompt: Sand is teeny tiny bits of…?
choices: Rock
Sugar
Wood
quiz.answer: Rock
quiz.say: Sand at the beach is made of teeny tiny broken bits. Bits of rock, sugar, or wood?
quiz.explain: Sand is rock that waves and weather broke into tiny bits.

quiz.prompt: Rocks break down into soil in…?
choices: Many years
One day
One second
quiz.answer: Many years
quiz.say: How long does it take for rocks to break down into soil? Many years, one day, or one second?
quiz.explain: Rocks break into soil very slowly, over many, many years.

lesson_media.alt: A rock cycle connects igneous rock, transported sediment, sedimentary rock, metamorphic rock, magma, and cooling back to igneous material.
lesson_media.caption: Any rock can enter multiple pathways when conditions change; the cycle is a network over long time, not one compulsory sequence.

nodes.title: The Water Cycle
nodes.goal: Evaporation, clouds, rain and rivers.
nodes.kid_text: When the Sun warms a puddle, the water sneaks up into the air as invisible mist called evaporation. Up high the mist cools and gathers into fluffy clouds, and when a cloud gets too full, water falls back down as rain. The rain runs into rivers and back to the sea, and then it starts all over again!

quiz.prompt: Sun warms a puddle. The water goes…?
choices: Up into the air
Down into the ground
Away forever
quiz.answer: Up into the air
quiz.say: The sun warms a puddle and the water sneaks away. Does it go up into the air, down into the ground, or away forever?
quiz.explain: Warm water rises into the air as invisible mist. None of it is lost.

quiz.prompt: A cloud gets too full. ☁️ What falls?
choices: Rain
Wind
Sunshine
quiz.answer: Rain
quiz.say: When a cloud gets too full of water, what falls down from it? Rain, wind, or sunshine?
quiz.explain: A full cloud lets its water fall back down as rain.

quiz.prompt: Rivers carry the water back to the…?
choices: Sea
Sky
Mountain top
quiz.answer: Sea
quiz.say: After rain fills the rivers, where does all that water end up? The sea, the sky, or a mountain top?
quiz.explain: Rivers run downhill to the sea, and then the whole cycle starts again.

quiz.prompt: Water sneaking into the air is…?
choices: Evaporation
Melting
Freezing
quiz.answer: Evaporation
quiz.say: When warm water sneaks up into the air as invisible mist, is that evaporation, melting, or freezing?
quiz.explain: Evaporation is water sneaking up into the air as mist.

quiz.prompt: Clouds are made of tiny…? ☁️
choices: Water drops
Bits of cotton
Puffs of smoke
quiz.answer: Water drops
quiz.say: What are fluffy clouds really made of? Water drops, bits of cotton, or puffs of smoke?
quiz.explain: Clouds are millions of tiny water drops, even though they look fluffy.

quiz.prompt: Wet clothes dry. The water went…? 👕
choices: Into the air
Into the ground
Into the cloth
quiz.answer: Into the air
quiz.say: Your wet shirt dries in the sunshine. Did the water go into the air, into the ground, or into the cloth?
quiz.explain: The sun warmed the water and it evaporated into the air.

quiz.prompt: Way up high, the misty air gets…?
choices: Cooler
Hotter
Drier
quiz.answer: Cooler
quiz.say: When the misty water floats way up high, does the air get cooler, hotter, or drier?
quiz.explain: Up high it is cooler, and cool air turns the mist into cloud drops.

lesson_media.alt: A five-part water cycle follows solar evaporation through condensation, precipitation, runoff, infiltration, and return to surface reservoirs.
lesson_media.caption: Water is conserved while changing state and reservoir; energy and gravity drive the transfers at very different rates.

nodes.title: The Changing Earth
nodes.goal: Volcanoes, earthquakes and mountains.

quiz.prompt: Earth's hard outer shell is broken into large moving pieces called tectonic plates. Along the west coast of South America, an ocean plate is slowly sliding underneath the continent. Which feature is this most likely to build there?
quiz.answer: A chain of volcanic mountains
quiz.explain: Where one plate dives beneath another, the crust is squeezed upward into mountains and magma rises to feed volcanoes, as along the Andes.
choices: A flat desert with no hills
A chain of volcanic mountains
A broad basin of calm lakes
A field of drifting sand dunes

quiz.prompt: During an earthquake, people far from the center often feel shaking a short while AFTER the ground first moves at the source. Why is there a delay?
quiz.answer: Seismic waves need time to travel out to distant places
quiz.explain: An earthquake releases seismic waves that spread through the ground at a limited speed, so distant locations shake later than the source.
choices: The ground far away shakes only once the crack has crept out to it
Seismic waves need time to travel out to distant places
The sound of the quake carries the shaking through the air
The shaking starts everywhere at once, and distant people notice it late

quiz.prompt: A tectonic plate creeps north at 5 centimetres per year, about as fast as a fingernail grows. How many centimetres does it travel in 20 years?
quiz.explain: 5 centimetres each year for 20 years gives 5 x 20 = 100 centimetres, or one whole metre.

quiz.prompt: Hikers near the top of a mountain range, hundreds of kilometres from any sea, find layers of rock packed with seashell fossils. What does this most likely show?
quiz.answer: Rock that formed under the sea was later pushed up
choices: Rock that formed under the sea was later pushed up
The shells grew inside the rock while it was cooling
Sea birds carried the shells up there over many centuries
The ocean once covered the planet right up to that height
quiz.explain: Sediment full of shells settled on an ancient sea floor, hardened into rock, and was later lifted thousands of metres by colliding plates.

quiz.prompt: A world map marking every earthquake of the past century shows them packed into narrow bands rather than scattered evenly. Why do they line up like that?
quiz.answer: They cluster along the edges where tectonic plates meet
choices: They cluster along the edges where tectonic plates meet
They follow the chains of volcanoes, since eruptions shake the ground
They occur wherever the land rises highest above the sea
They mark where the crust is thinnest and breaks most easily
quiz.explain: Plates grind past, pull away from, or dive under one another at their boundaries, and that is where the stress builds and releases as earthquakes.

quiz.prompt: Two volcanoes erupt on the same island. One pours out runny lava that spreads for kilometres before hardening. The other squeezes out thick, sticky lava that barely flows before it stops. What shape will the second volcano most likely build?
quiz.answer: A steep, cone-shaped peak
choices: A steep, cone-shaped peak
A wide, gently sloping dome
A flat sheet of rock spread over the island
A deep pit with no raised rim around it
quiz.explain: Sticky lava cannot travel far, so it piles up close to the vent and builds a steep cone; runny lava spreads out into a broad, low shield.

quiz.prompt: Two plates pull apart from each other at 4 centimetres a year. How many centimetres wider is the gap after 250 years?
quiz.explain: 4 x 250 = 1,000 centimetres, which is 10 metres.

quiz.prompt: A steep-sided valley far inland is strewn with rounded boulders of a rock found only in mountains 100 kilometres to the north. What most likely carried them there?
quiz.answer: A glacier that once filled the valley
choices: A glacier that once filled the valley
A single enormous flood sweeping down the valley
Wind blowing over many thousands of years
A volcano that hurled them that far north
quiz.explain: Ice can drag boulders of any size for great distances and leaves them scattered when it melts. Wind moves only fine grains, and rivers sort material by size.

quiz.prompt: An old stone carving is still sharp on the sheltered side of a church but blurred and crumbly on the side facing the wind and rain. Which process explains the blurring?
quiz.answer: Weathering
choices: Weathering
Erosion
Deposition
Compaction
quiz.explain: Weathering is the breakdown of rock in place by water, frost, air and living things, and it works hardest where the weather reaches. Erosion is the carrying away of the loosened material afterwards.

quiz.prompt: Two towns are the same distance from the centre of an earthquake, yet one is wrecked and the other is barely marked. Give two reasons this can happen.
quiz.answer: The shaking depends on the ground as well as the quake: soft loose ground shakes far harder than solid rock. It also depends on the buildings, because houses that are braced and tied together stay up while unbraced ones fall.
quiz.explain: Earthquake damage is a product of the shaking, the local ground and the buildings. That is why engineering and geology matter as much as the size of the quake.

lesson_media.alt: Divergent, convergent, and transform boundary panels connect relative plate motion to ridges, subduction, mountains, volcanoes, and earthquakes.
lesson_media.caption: Tectonic hazards are surface expressions of moving lithospheric plates and accumulated stress, not random events scattered evenly over Earth.

nodes.title: Weather and Climate
nodes.goal: The atmosphere, weather systems and climate zones.

quiz.prompt: A town near the equator has hot temperatures and heavy rain almost every day, all year round. A town near the North Pole is frozen most of the year. What best explains this difference in climate?
quiz.answer: The Sun's rays strike the equator more directly
quiz.explain: Near the equator the Sun's rays hit almost straight down, concentrating energy, while near the poles the same rays spread over a larger, more slanted area.
choices: The poles lean away from the Sun all year and never warm up
The equator is much closer to the Sun than the poles are
The equator has thinner air, which traps heat more easily
The Sun's rays strike the equator more directly

quiz.prompt: Weather and climate are related but different. Which statement correctly distinguishes them?
quiz.answer: Weather is today's atmosphere; climate is the long-term average
quiz.explain: Weather is the short-term condition on a given day, while climate is the long-term average of weather in a place over decades.
choices: Weather and climate are two names for exactly the same thing
Weather is today's atmosphere; climate is the long-term average
Weather describes a single country, while climate describes the entire planet
Weather is the average over years; climate is what happens today

quiz.prompt: Air usually cools by about 6 degrees Celsius for every 1,000 metres you climb. A valley town sits at 20 degrees Celsius. What temperature, in degrees Celsius, would you expect at a hut 2,000 metres higher up the mountain?
quiz.explain: Climbing 2,000 metres means two lots of 6 degrees, a fall of 12 degrees, so 20 - 12 = 8 degrees Celsius.

quiz.prompt: A forecaster says a cold front will reach a town this evening. Ahead of it the air is warm and damp; behind it the air is cold and dense. As the cold air wedges in underneath, what usually happens?
quiz.answer: The warm air is shoved upward, cooling until clouds and rain form
choices: The warm air is shoved upward, cooling until clouds and rain form
The warm air is pressed downward and the sky clears at once
The two air masses blend and the weather stays unchanged
The cold air soaks into the ground and warms up again by morning
quiz.explain: Dense cold air slides under warm moist air and lifts it; the rising air cools, its water vapour condenses, and a band of cloud and rain forms along the front.

quiz.prompt: A hiker screws the cap onto an empty plastic bottle at the top of a high mountain, then carries it down to the coast. On arrival the bottle is dented and crumpled. Why?
quiz.answer: Air presses harder at sea level than it did up the mountain
choices: Air presses harder at sea level than it did up the mountain
The air sealed inside the bottle cooled down and shrank away
The plastic softened in the warmer air lower down the mountain
Water vapour leaked out through the plastic during the walk
quiz.explain: There is more air above you at sea level, so outside pressure is higher there; the thin mountain air trapped inside cannot push back as hard and the bottle collapses inward.

quiz.prompt: Two cities lie at exactly the same latitude. One sits on the coast; the other lies far inland. Compared with the coastal city, what should the inland city's temperatures look like across the year?
quiz.answer: Warmer summers and colder winters
choices: Warmer summers and colder winters
Cooler summers and milder winters
Almost the same temperature in every season
Colder summers together with warmer winters
quiz.explain: Water heats and cools far more slowly than land, so the sea steadies a coastal city's temperature; inland cities swing to bigger extremes both ways.

quiz.prompt: Dry air cools by about 10 degrees Celsius for every 1,000 metres it rises. Air at sea level is 25 degrees Celsius. What temperature, in degrees Celsius, is it after rising 1,500 metres?
quiz.explain: Rising 1,500 metres cools the air by 1.5 x 10 = 15 degrees, so 25 - 15 = 10 degrees Celsius.

quiz.prompt: A glass of iced drink left on a table on a warm day goes wet all over the outside. Where does that water come from?
quiz.answer: Water vapour in the air condenses on the cold glass
choices: The ice melts and runs over the rim
Water vapour in the air condenses on the cold glass
Water works its way slowly out through the glass wall
The cold somehow makes brand-new water on the surface
quiz.explain: Warm air holds invisible water vapour. Chilled against the cold surface it can hold less, so the extra turns back into liquid on the outside of the glass.

quiz.prompt: Clouds and rain pile up on the side of a mountain range that the wind hits, while the far side stays dry. What is the best explanation?
quiz.answer: Air rises and cools, dropping its rain before it descends
choices: Mountains simply block the clouds from crossing
Air rises and cools, dropping its rain before it descends
The far side of the range is always the warmer of the two
Wind speeds up over the summit and blows the clouds right away
quiz.explain: Rising air cools, so its water vapour condenses and falls. The air that descends the far side has already lost that water and warms as it sinks.

quiz.prompt: Two evenings start at the same temperature. One night is cloudy and the morning is mild; the other is clear and the morning is frosty. Why?
quiz.answer: Clouds trap heat radiating up from the ground
choices: Clouds trap heat radiating up from the ground
A clear sky lets the cold of space sink down to the ground
Clouds are warmer than the air that surrounds them
Frost forms only when the air is unusually damp
quiz.explain: The ground radiates heat away all night. Cloud absorbs much of it and sends some back down, so cloudy nights cool far less than clear ones.

lesson_media.alt: A vertical atmosphere profile places weather in the troposphere, ozone heating in the stratosphere, meteors in the mesosphere, and thin thermospheric air above.
lesson_media.caption: Atmospheric layers differ in temperature trend and composition; climate describes long-term statistics of the variable weather below.

nodes.title: Worlds of the Solar System
nodes.goal: Each planet's character; comets and asteroids.

quiz.prompt: Jupiter is a giant planet made mostly of gas, while Mars is a small rocky planet. If you tried to stand on each, what would you find?
quiz.answer: Mars has a solid rocky surface; Jupiter has none
quiz.explain: Mars is a terrestrial (rocky) planet with a solid crust, while Jupiter is a gas giant with no solid surface to stand on.
choices: Jupiter has solid ground beneath its clouds; Mars has none
Both have firm rocky ground just like Earth does
Neither can be stood on, since both are gas the whole way down
Mars has a solid rocky surface; Jupiter has none

quiz.prompt: A comet swings close to the Sun and grows a long glowing tail, then the tail shrinks as it moves far away again. What causes the tail?
quiz.answer: Solar heat vaporizes the comet's ices into gas and dust
quiz.explain: As a comet nears the Sun, solar heat turns its ices to gas and the solar wind and radiation push that gas and dust into a tail pointing away from the Sun.
choices: Dust is scraped off the comet by its speed and left trailing behind
The comet catches fire rubbing against the air in space
The comet's ice melts and the water trails away behind it
Solar heat vaporizes the comet's ices into gas and dust

quiz.prompt: Mars takes about 687 Earth days to travel once around the Sun. Earth takes about 365 days. How many more days does one Mars year last than one Earth year?
quiz.explain: 687 - 365 = 322 days. Mars is farther out, so it has a longer path to travel and moves more slowly along it.

quiz.prompt: Gravity at the surface of Mars pulls with about 0.38 times the strength of Earth's. A rover weighs 900 newtons on Earth. About how many newtons would the same rover weigh on Mars?
quiz.explain: 900 x 0.38 = 342 newtons. The rover's material never changes, but weaker gravity means a smaller pull.

quiz.prompt: Mercury orbits closest to the Sun, yet Venus, the next planet out, has the hottest surface of any planet. What best explains this?
quiz.answer: A thick blanket of atmosphere holds Venus's heat in
choices: A thick blanket of atmosphere holds Venus's heat in
Venus passes closer to the Sun than Mercury does at times
Erupting volcanoes keep the whole surface of Venus molten
Venus is the larger planet, so it stores far more solar heat
quiz.explain: Venus is wrapped in a dense carbon-dioxide atmosphere that traps heat, while Mercury is almost airless and radiates its heat straight back to space.

quiz.prompt: A rocky, cratered object about 20 kilometres across is tracked orbiting between Mars and Jupiter. Even at its closest approach to the Sun it never grows a tail. What is it?
quiz.answer: An asteroid, made mostly of rock and metal with little ice
choices: An asteroid, made mostly of rock and metal with little ice
A comet whose tail happens to point directly behind it
A tiny planet that lost its atmosphere to the solar wind
A meteor that is slowly burning up as it travels
quiz.explain: Comet tails come from ices boiling off near the Sun. An object that stays tailless in the inner solar system holds little ice, which marks it as a rocky asteroid.

quiz.prompt: Jupiter takes about 12 Earth years to go once around the Sun. About how many Jupiter years pass during 60 Earth years?
quiz.explain: 60 divided by 12 gives 5 complete Jupiter orbits.

quiz.prompt: Saturn orbits about 9.5 astronomical units from the Sun, and Earth orbits at 1 astronomical unit. How many times further from the Sun is Saturn than Earth?
quiz.explain: 9.5 divided by 1 is 9.5 times as far.

quiz.prompt: On Venus, a single spin on its axis takes longer than one trip around the Sun. What does that tell you?
quiz.answer: Venus turns on its axis more slowly than it travels around the Sun
choices: Venus takes longer to orbit the Sun than any other planet
Venus turns on its axis more slowly than it travels around the Sun
Venus does not turn on its axis at all, and only travels around the Sun
Venus lies so far from the Sun that its year is stretched out
quiz.explain: A day is one spin and a year is one orbit. On Venus the spin is the slower of the two, which is why its day outlasts its year.

quiz.prompt: Every planet orbits the Sun in nearly the same flat plane and in the same direction. Which idea does this pattern support best?
quiz.answer: They formed together out of one spinning disc of material
choices: They formed together out of one spinning disc of material
They were each captured one at a time by the Sun's gravity
Sunlight slowly pushed them into line over billions of years
Collisions between the young planets settled all their orbits
quiz.explain: Captured bodies would arrive on random, tilted orbits. A shared plane and direction is the signature of a single rotating cloud that flattened as it collapsed.

lesson_media.alt: Three planetary families compare rocky terrestrial worlds, gas and ice giants, and smaller asteroids and comets by composition and structure.
lesson_media.caption: Planet categories reveal formation patterns without erasing diversity: nearby size or distance alone does not determine a world's history.

nodes.title: Stars and Galaxies
nodes.goal: What stars are; the Milky Way.

quiz.prompt: Our Sun is a star, yet it looks far bigger and brighter than the stars we see at night. Why do those night-time stars look like tiny points of light instead?
quiz.answer: They lie vastly farther away from us than the Sun
quiz.explain: Other stars are similar to or larger than the Sun, but they lie trillions of kilometers away, so their light reaches us as faint points.
choices: They are dimmed by Earth's thick atmosphere
They are much smaller balls of gas than our own Sun
They are burning out, so only a little light is left
They lie vastly farther away from us than the Sun

quiz.prompt: On a very dark night away from city lights, you can see a hazy band of light stretching across the sky, sometimes called the Milky Way. What is that band?
quiz.answer: The blended light of billions of stars in our galaxy
quiz.explain: The Milky Way band is our galaxy seen edge-on, its light coming from countless stars too far to see individually.
choices: The blended light of billions of stars in our galaxy
A high, thin cloud of water vapour drifting across the sky
Another galaxy far off, seen edge-on from outside it
A glowing cloud of gas and dust with no stars in it

quiz.prompt: Our galaxy is a disc about 100,000 light-years across, and the Sun sits about 26,000 light-years from the centre. Measuring straight outward from the Sun, how many light-years away is the outer edge of the disc?
quiz.explain: The disc's radius is half of 100,000, which is 50,000 light-years. Subtracting the Sun's 26,000 leaves 24,000 light-years to the rim.

quiz.prompt: One light-year is about 9.5 trillion kilometres. The star Vega lies about 25 light-years from Earth. How many trillion kilometres away is Vega?
quiz.explain: 25 x 9.5 = 237.5 trillion kilometres. A light-year measures distance, not time, even though its name mentions years.

quiz.prompt: A long-exposure photograph of a star cluster shows some stars glowing blue-white and others a deep orange-red. What does that colour difference mainly reveal?
quiz.answer: How hot each star's surface is
choices: How hot each star's surface is
How far each star lies from us
How much dust surrounds each star
How many planets circle each star
quiz.explain: Hotter surfaces glow blue-white and cooler ones glow red, in the same way a poker glows red when warm and white when hotter still.

quiz.prompt: A friend says the Sun must sit at the centre of the Milky Way, because it is the most important star to us. Which correction fits what astronomers have measured?
quiz.answer: The Sun is an ordinary star far out along one spiral arm
choices: The Sun is an ordinary star far out along one spiral arm
The Sun sits at the centre, which is why it outshines the rest
The Sun lies outside the Milky Way, which is a separate object
The Sun must be near the centre, since stars look evenly spread
quiz.explain: The Sun is an unremarkable star about half way out from the galactic centre; it looks brilliant only because it sits so close to us.

quiz.prompt: Proxima Centauri lies about 4.2 light-years from Earth. How many years does its light take to reach us?
quiz.explain: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, so light from 4.2 light-years away has been travelling 4.2 years.

quiz.prompt: The Sun is about 150 million kilometres away and light travels 300,000 kilometres each second. How many seconds does sunlight take to reach Earth?
quiz.explain: 150,000,000 divided by 300,000 is 500 seconds, which is 8 minutes and 20 seconds.

quiz.prompt: Two stars look equally bright in the night sky, but one of them is far further away than the other. What must be true of the distant one?
quiz.answer: It gives out much more light than the nearer star
choices: It gives out much more light than the nearer star
It must be a good deal cooler than the nearer star
It must have formed more recently than the nearer star
It must be exactly the same kind of star as the nearer one
quiz.explain: Brightness in the sky depends on how much light a star makes and how far away it is. To look the same from further off, it must be making much more light.

quiz.prompt: The stars of a constellation trace a shape from Earth, yet they are not near one another in space. Why do they still look grouped?
quiz.answer: They happen to lie in nearly the same direction from Earth
choices: They are held together by their own gravity
They happen to lie in nearly the same direction from Earth
They all shine out with very nearly the same true brightness
They all formed out of one and the same cloud of gas long ago
quiz.explain: A constellation is a line-of-sight effect. Its stars can be at wildly different distances and are usually unconnected.

lesson_media.alt: A nested cosmic scale places Earth by the Sun, nearby stars, the Milky Way with hundreds of billions of stars, and the galaxy-rich Local Group.
lesson_media.caption: Stars and galaxies occupy different hierarchy levels: the Sun is one star inside a galaxy, not a separate kind of object from other stars.

nodes.title: Oceans and Rivers
nodes.goal: The water planet: currents, tides and life.

quiz.prompt: At a beach, the water slowly creeps up the sand for about six hours, then slowly retreats for about six hours, twice a day. What mainly causes this rise and fall of the tides?
quiz.answer: The gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun on the oceans
quiz.explain: The Moon's gravity, aided by the Sun's, tugs on ocean water and creates bulges that we experience as high and low tides as Earth rotates.
choices: Steady daytime winds pushing the water up the beach
The Sun heating the sea by day, so the water swells up the sand
Water sloshing from side to side as Earth spins on its axis
The gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun on the oceans

quiz.prompt: Ocean currents act like giant rivers within the sea. A warm current flowing from the tropics toward a cold northern coast would most likely have what effect on that coast?
quiz.answer: Make its climate milder than its latitude alone suggests
quiz.explain: Warm currents carry heat from the tropics, warming the air over nearby coasts and giving them milder climates than their latitude alone would suggest.
choices: Make its climate milder than its latitude alone suggests
Warm the sea itself but leave the air above it unchanged
Have little effect, since it cools long before it arrives
Bring tropical summers but leave the winters just as cold

quiz.prompt: A harbour tide gauge reads 0.4 metres at low tide and 2.8 metres at high tide. What is the tidal range, in metres?
quiz.explain: The tidal range is the difference between high and low water: 2.8 - 0.4 = 2.4 metres.

quiz.prompt: A ball floats offshore while waves roll past underneath it. The ball bobs up and down again and again but drifts hardly at all toward the beach. What does this show about a water wave?
quiz.answer: Its energy moves forward while the water mostly rises and falls
choices: Its energy moves forward while the water mostly rises and falls
The same water travels the whole way from far out to the beach
The ball is too light for the moving water to carry it along
Only the surface layer moves forward; the water below stays still
quiz.explain: A wave transports energy, not water. Each parcel of water circles roughly in place, so a float rises and falls without being carried to shore.

quiz.prompt: A mountain stream tumbles along carrying sand and gravel. Where it widens and slows as it enters the sea, what happens to that load?
quiz.answer: It settles out and builds new land at the river mouth
choices: It settles out and builds new land at the river mouth
It dissolves into the seawater and disappears completely
It is swept onward unchanged into the deep open ocean
It turns into the salt that makes seawater taste salty
quiz.explain: Fast water can carry heavy particles; as the current slows the largest grains drop first, piling into sandbanks and deltas.

quiz.prompt: Rivers taste fresh, yet they pour into an ocean that is salty. How did the sea come to hold so much salt?
quiz.answer: Rivers deliver dissolved salt, and evaporation leaves it behind
choices: Rivers deliver dissolved salt, and evaporation leaves it behind
Rain on the ocean is salty, while the rivers stay fresh
Sea creatures make salt and release it steadily into the water
The sea has been just as salty since the day it first formed
quiz.explain: Rivers dissolve tiny amounts of mineral salt from rock and carry it seaward; water evaporates from the ocean but the salt cannot, so it accumulates.

quiz.prompt: A river carries 300 kilograms of sediment past a bridge every minute. How many kilograms pass in one hour?
quiz.explain: 300 x 60 = 18,000 kilograms in an hour.

quiz.prompt: Coral reefs grow in shallow, clear tropical water rather than in the deep sea. Which reason fits best?
quiz.answer: The tiny algae living inside the coral need sunlight
choices: The pressure of deep water would crush the coral's stony skeleton
The tiny algae living inside the coral need sunlight
Coral needs waves breaking over it in order to survive
Deep water carries none of the minerals needed for building
quiz.explain: Reef-building corals house photosynthetic algae that feed them, so the coral can only thrive where enough light reaches.

quiz.prompt: Over a year, one end of a beach loses sand while the other end gains it. What is most likely happening?
quiz.answer: Waves arriving at an angle drag sand along the shore
choices: The beach is sinking at one end and rising at the other
The tide carries the sand out and back again each day
Waves arriving at an angle drag sand along the shore
Wind picks the sand up and drops it at the other end
quiz.explain: This is longshore drift. Waves run up the beach at an angle and drain straight back, so each swash moves grains a little way along the coast.

quiz.prompt: Explain why the sea warms up more slowly in summer, and cools more slowly in winter, than the land beside it.
quiz.answer: Water needs far more heat than rock or soil to change its temperature by the same amount, and waves and currents mix the warmth down through a deep layer instead of leaving it all at the surface. Both effects make the sea change temperature slowly.
quiz.explain: The sea's thermal inertia is why coastal places have milder summers and winters than inland places at the same latitude.

lesson_media.alt: An ocean network separates wind-driven surface currents and density-driven sinking and return flow from a distinct Moon-to-tides gravitational branch.
lesson_media.caption: Ocean motion combines multiple mechanisms; identifying the driver prevents tides, waves, currents, and river flow from being treated as one process.

nodes.title: Caring for Earth
nodes.goal: Resources, pollution and conservation.

quiz.prompt: A town gets its water from a river. A factory upstream begins dumping waste chemicals into the same river. This is an example of pollution because it:
quiz.answer: Adds harmful substances that damage the environment
quiz.explain: Pollution is the release of harmful materials into the environment, and contaminated river water can harm ecosystems and the communities downstream.
choices: Dilutes into so much water that it stops being harmful
Affects the factory's own land but not the town downstream
Changes how the river looks without harming what lives in it
Adds harmful substances that damage the environment

quiz.prompt: A forest is home to many rare animals, but people want its wood and land. Which action best reflects conservation?
quiz.answer: Protecting part of the forest and harvesting what regrows
quiz.explain: Conservation seeks to use resources sustainably and protect habitats so both nature and people benefit over the long term.
choices: Fencing the whole forest off so that no one may ever enter
Protecting part of the forest and harvesting what regrows
Moving the rare animals to a zoo and then clearing the land
Clearing the forest but planting the same number of trees elsewhere

quiz.prompt: A town of 4,000 people each throws away 2 kilograms of rubbish a day. A recycling scheme cuts that total by one quarter. How many kilograms of rubbish does the town throw away each day afterwards?
quiz.explain: 4,000 x 2 = 8,000 kilograms a day. A quarter of 8,000 is 2,000, so 8,000 - 2,000 = 6,000 kilograms remain.

quiz.prompt: A country compares two ways of making electricity: burning coal dug from underground, or turning turbines with wind. Which statement about the coal is correct?
quiz.answer: It will run out, since coal forms far slower than we burn it
choices: It will run out, since coal forms far slower than we burn it
It is renewable, since fresh coal keeps forming underground
It will last for ever, because Earth is such an enormous planet
It is renewable in the way wind is, since both come from nature
quiz.explain: Coal took hundreds of millions of years to form from buried plants. We burn it far faster than it is replaced, which makes it a non-renewable resource.

quiz.prompt: The last members of a rare frog species live in one small forest, and loggers plan to clear it. Ecologists warn that the species could be lost for good. What makes a species with a single small habitat so vulnerable?
quiz.answer: There is nowhere else it can live if that one place is destroyed
choices: There is nowhere else it can live if that one place is destroyed
The frogs would simply hop to another forest and settle there
The frogs would swiftly change into a new species that copes
A few frogs kept safe in a zoo would be enough to save the species
quiz.explain: A species confined to one site has no back-up population, so a single fire, flood or clearance can end it everywhere at once.

quiz.prompt: A pesticide sprayed on farmland washes into a lake. Tiny water plants absorb a little of it, small fish eat great numbers of those plants, and pike eat great numbers of the small fish. The chemical is not broken down or excreted. Where would you expect to find the most pesticide inside one animal?
quiz.answer: In a pike
choices: In a pike
In a small fish
In algae
Spread evenly between plant, fish and pike
quiz.explain: Each animal keeps the pesticide from everything it eats, so the chemical concentrates as it climbs the food chain and peaks in the top predator.

quiz.prompt: A house uses 12 kilowatt-hours of electricity a day, and its solar panels supply 9 kilowatt-hours a day. What percentage of its electricity comes from the panels?
quiz.explain: 9 divided by 12 is 0.75, which is 75 percent.

quiz.prompt: A city plants thousands of trees along its streets. Besides looking pleasant, which effect is best supported by evidence?
quiz.answer: Cooler streets and cleaner air
choices: Cooler streets and cleaner air
Cleaner air but hotter streets, since trees block the breeze
Heavier rainfall across the whole region
Warmer buildings in winter
quiz.explain: Tree canopies shade surfaces and release water vapour, lowering street temperatures, and their leaves trap some airborne particles.

quiz.prompt: Aluminium cans can be melted down and reused over and over, but each round of paper recycling leaves the fibres shorter. What follows from this?
quiz.answer: Paper can be recycled only a limited number of times
choices: Paper can be recycled only a limited number of times
There is no point putting paper out for recycling at all
Both can be recycled endlessly, just at different costs
Aluminium should be thrown away, since paper recycles more easily
quiz.explain: Metals keep their properties through melting, so recycling is effectively endless. Paper fibres degrade, so recycled paper eventually needs fresh fibre mixed in.

quiz.prompt: Two nature reserves are separated by a motorway, and ecologists ask for a wildlife bridge between them. Which problem are they trying to solve?
quiz.answer: Small cut-off populations are far more likely to die out
choices: Animals crossing the road at ground level are killed by traffic
Small cut-off populations are far more likely to die out
Each reserve on its own is too small an area to hold the animals
The animals need to reach drinking water on the far side
quiz.explain: Splitting a habitat leaves small isolated groups that lose variety and can be wiped out by one bad year. A crossing restores the movement between them.

lesson_media.alt: An environmental action matrix links climate emissions, water pollution, and habitat loss to source-level interventions and measurable ecological responses.
lesson_media.caption: Effective care targets causes and tracks outcomes; visible clean-up alone may leave the upstream pressure unchanged.

nodes.title: Earth Science
nodes.goal: Rock cycle, deep time and Earth's interior.

quiz.prompt: A geologist finds a layer of sandstone. Grains in it were once part of an older granite mountain that eroded, washed to a river delta, and were buried and cemented. If this sandstone is later dragged deep underground and subjected to intense heat and pressure without melting, what will it most likely become?
quiz.answer: A metamorphic rock such as quartzite
quiz.explain: Heat and pressure that alter a rock without melting it produce metamorphic rock; sandstone recrystallizes into quartzite.
choices: Sandstone again, only harder and more tightly cemented
Igneous granite, since its grains came from granite originally
Magma, because rock at that depth is always molten
A metamorphic rock such as quartzite

quiz.prompt: In an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary rock layers, a fossil of a simple shelled animal is found in a lower layer and a fossil of a fish is found in a higher layer. Using the principle of superposition, what can you conclude?
quiz.answer: The shelled animal lived earlier than the fish
quiz.explain: In undisturbed layers, lower beds were deposited first, so fossils in deeper layers are older than those above them.
choices: The shelled animal lived earlier than the fish
The fish lived earlier than the shelled animal
Both organisms lived at exactly the same time
The layers formed from top to bottom, so the fish is oldest

quiz.prompt: Seismic waves travel faster through denser, more rigid material. Waves passing through Earth's interior speed up sharply at a certain depth, then slow when they reach the outer core. What does this tell scientists?
quiz.answer: Earth is layered, with different density and state at depth
quiz.explain: Changes in seismic wave speed and direction reveal boundaries between crust, mantle, and core, showing Earth's layered structure.
choices: Earth is a uniform ball of the same rock throughout
Earth is layered, with different density and state at depth
Everything below the crust is molten, all the way down
Seismic waves lose energy with distance, so they simply slow down

quiz.prompt: Mud settles on a quiet lake bed at an average rate of 0.5 millimetres per year. How many years would it take to build up a layer 2 metres thick?
quiz.explain: 2 metres is 2,000 millimetres, and 2,000 / 0.5 = 4,000 years. Slow rates over long spans build thick sequences, which is how deep time works.

quiz.prompt: The oldest rocks on the continents are close to 4 billion years old, but nowhere on the ocean floor is the crust older than about 200 million years. Explain why.
quiz.answer: Ocean crust is made continuously at mid-ocean ridges and destroyed at subduction zones, so it is recycled back into the mantle within roughly 200 million years. Continental crust is less dense and buoyant, so it resists subduction and survives for billions of years.
quiz.explain: Sea floor is conveyor-belt crust: created at ridges, consumed at trenches. Continental rock is too buoyant to be dragged down, so it accumulates age.

quiz.prompt: A cliff face shows three sedimentary layers. A vertical sheet of granite cuts straight across all three, but the layer lying on top of them runs unbroken over the granite. Which order of events does the cliff record?
quiz.answer: The three lower layers, then the granite, then the top layer
choices: The granite first, then all four layers settled around it
The three lower layers, then the granite, then the top layer
The top layer, then the granite, then the three lower layers
All four layers and the granite formed in one single event
quiz.explain: A feature that cuts a rock must be younger than it, and a layer that seals a feature must be younger still, which fixes the sequence.

quiz.prompt: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 5,730 years. A sample now holds one-eighth of its original amount of that isotope. How many years old is it?
quiz.explain: One-eighth remains after three half-lives, and 3 x 5,730 = 17,190 years.

quiz.prompt: A river cuts down through bedrock at 0.2 millimetres per year. How many metres deep is the gorge after 1 million years?
quiz.explain: 0.2 mm x 1,000,000 = 200,000 mm, which is 200 metres.

quiz.prompt: A core drilled through a lake bed shows fine pale layers alternating with dark ones, one pair for each year. What can be read directly from the core?
quiz.answer: The number of years the layers took to accumulate
choices: The number of years the layers took to accumulate
The chemistry of the bedrock beneath the layers
The temperature of the lake in each year a pair formed
How deep the lake water had been when it first formed
quiz.explain: Annual layers, or varves, can be counted like tree rings, giving a year-by-year clock through the sediment.

quiz.prompt: Two rock outcrops 300 kilometres apart both contain the same distinctive volcanic ash bed. What is the strongest use a geologist can make of this?
quiz.answer: The two outcrops can be tied to the same moment in time
choices: The two outcrops were once joined and have drifted apart
The two outcrops can be tied to the same moment in time
The two outcrops must both lie close to an ancient volcano
The layers above the ash must be identical at both sites
quiz.explain: An ash fall is laid down almost instantly over a huge area, making it an excellent marker horizon for correlating separated rock sequences.

lesson_media.alt: A concentric Earth cross-section labels crust, slowly flowing solid mantle, liquid outer core, and pressure-solidified inner core with evidence-linked properties.
lesson_media.caption: Earth's rock cycle couples internal heat and plate tectonics to surface water, atmosphere, gravity, and immense geological time.

nodes.title: Astronomy
nodes.goal: Stellar life cycles, the scale of the cosmos.

quiz.prompt: Our Sun is a medium-mass star currently fusing hydrogen into helium. Based on stellar evolution, what is the most likely sequence of stages it will pass through as it ages and runs out of core hydrogen?
quiz.answer: Red giant, then a white dwarf after shedding its layers
quiz.explain: A Sun-like star swells into a red giant, expels its outer layers as a planetary nebula, and leaves behind a white dwarf; only much more massive stars end as supernovae.
choices: It explodes as a supernova and becomes a black hole
Red giant, then a white dwarf after shedding its layers
It stays exactly the same star for the rest of time
It collapses instantly into a rapidly spinning neutron star

quiz.prompt: Light travels about 300,000 kilometers per second. A star is 4 light-years away, meaning its light takes 4 years to reach us. If the star suddenly brightened today, how many years from now would observers on Earth first see the change? Give the number of years.
quiz.explain: Because the light takes 4 years to cross the distance, we see any change 4 years after it actually happens.

quiz.prompt: A newer telescope has a mirror four times the diameter of an older one. Compared with the smaller telescope, the larger one can:
quiz.answer: Gather far more light and reveal fainter objects
quiz.explain: A larger mirror collects more light (proportional to its area), letting a telescope detect fainter and farther objects and resolve finer detail.
choices: Magnify images further without collecting extra light
Gather far more light and reveal fainter objects
Make distant objects appear sixteen times closer
Take in a much wider field, showing more sky at once

quiz.prompt: Sunlight takes 8.3 minutes to travel the 1 astronomical unit (AU) from the Sun to Earth. Jupiter orbits at 5.2 AU. How many minutes does sunlight take to reach Jupiter? Round to the nearest whole minute.
quiz.explain: 8.3 x 5.2 = 43.2 minutes. Light speed is fixed, so travel time scales directly with distance.

quiz.prompt: Star A has ten times the Sun's mass; Star B has half of it. Astronomers expect one of them to still be shining long after the other has died. Which one, and why?
quiz.answer: Star B, because it burns its smaller fuel supply very slowly
choices: Star B, because it burns its smaller fuel supply very slowly
Star A, because it started out with ten times as much fuel
Star A, because heavier stars fuse at a steadier, gentler rate
Star B, because a cooler star loses its heat far more slowly
quiz.explain: A massive star's crushing core pressure drives fusion enormously faster, so despite having more fuel it lasts only millions of years, while a red dwarf lasts far longer than the present age of the universe.

quiz.prompt: Ground telescopes can be built with mirrors many times larger than anything launched into orbit, yet astronomers still spend billions putting telescopes in space. What do they gain?
quiz.answer: A view unblurred by air, and light the atmosphere blocks
choices: A view unblurred by air, and light the atmosphere blocks
A position thousands of kilometres nearer the stars observed
Escape from Earth's gravity, which otherwise bends the starlight
A mirror that can be built far larger than any on the ground
quiz.explain: Turbulent air smears star images and the atmosphere absorbs most ultraviolet, X-ray and much infrared light, so orbiting instruments see sharper and across far more of the spectrum.

quiz.prompt: A star's parallax is measured as 0.05 arcseconds. Distance in parsecs is 1 divided by the parallax in arcseconds. Give the distance in parsecs.
quiz.explain: 1 divided by 0.05 is 20 parsecs.

quiz.prompt: Apparent brightness falls off with the square of distance. Two identical stars are observed, and star B is 3 times as far away as star A. How many times fainter does star B appear?
quiz.explain: Brightness scales as one over distance squared, so three times the distance gives 3 squared = 9 times fainter.

quiz.prompt: A star's spectrum shows strong hydrogen lines but almost no lines of heavier elements. Which conclusion is best supported?
quiz.answer: It formed early, from gas not yet enriched by earlier stars
choices: It is far hotter than the Sun
It formed early, from gas not yet enriched by earlier stars
It is an unusually young star that only formed quite recently
It contains not one element heavier than hydrogen anywhere in it
quiz.explain: Heavy elements are manufactured by earlier generations of stars. A star poor in them formed from gas that had not yet been enriched, so it is old.

quiz.prompt: A star dims by 1 percent every 3 days, and each dip has the same depth, the same duration and a flat bottom. Which explanation fits best?
quiz.answer: A planet crosses the star's disc once each orbit
choices: The star pulsates, swelling and shrinking
A planet crosses the star's disc once each orbit
A dust cloud drifts across the line of sight
Starspots rotate into and out of view
quiz.explain: Strict repetition with an identical flat-bottomed profile is the signature of a transit. Pulsations and spots give smoother, less repeatable light curves.

lesson_media.alt: A stellar-evolution branch contrasts low-mass stars ending as white dwarfs with high-mass stars reaching supernovae and compact remnants.
lesson_media.caption: Astronomy infers life cycles by comparing many stars and uses overlapping distance methods to establish the scale of the cosmos.

nodes.title: Climate Science
nodes.goal: The greenhouse effect and climate change.

quiz.prompt: Certain gases in the atmosphere, like carbon dioxide, let sunlight through to warm the ground but absorb some of the heat the ground radiates back out. If the concentration of these gases increases, what is the expected result?
quiz.answer: The lower atmosphere traps more heat and warms
quiz.explain: Greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared radiation; increasing them enhances the greenhouse effect and warms the planet.
choices: The lower atmosphere traps more heat and warms
Sunlight is blocked high in the atmosphere, so the surface cools
The ozone hole widens, letting extra heat reach the ground
Heat is held only until nightfall, when it all escapes again

quiz.prompt: Burning coal, oil, and gas moves carbon that was locked underground for millions of years into the atmosphere as CO2. In terms of the carbon cycle, why does this raise atmospheric CO2 faster than natural processes can remove it?
quiz.answer: It adds carbon faster than oceans and plants can absorb it
quiz.explain: Fossil fuel burning releases stored carbon much faster than natural sinks like oceans and forests can take it up, so CO2 accumulates.
choices: It adds carbon faster than oceans and plants can absorb it
Plants take up the extra carbon faster than it appears
Volcanoes release far more carbon dioxide than fuel burning does
The oceans absorb whatever the air cannot hold, keeping it steady

quiz.prompt: As Arctic sea ice melts, bright white ice is replaced by dark open ocean. Dark water absorbs more sunlight than reflective ice. What kind of effect does this create?
quiz.answer: A reinforcing feedback that speeds up further melting
quiz.explain: Losing reflective ice lowers Earth's albedo, so more heat is absorbed, causing more melting in a self-reinforcing (positive) feedback.
choices: A balancing effect that cools the Arctic back down
A reinforcing feedback that speeds up further melting
A delayed effect that shows up only centuries from now
A one-time change with no further effect on temperature

quiz.prompt: Atmospheric carbon dioxide stood near 280 parts per million before the industrial era and is near 420 parts per million today. By what percentage has it risen?
quiz.explain: The rise is 420 - 280 = 140 ppm, and 140 / 280 = 0.5, which is a 50 percent increase over the pre-industrial level.

quiz.prompt: After two bitterly cold winters in a row, a newspaper column claims that global warming has been disproved. Which reply rests on the strongest scientific ground?
quiz.answer: Climate is a decades-long average, so two cold winters settle little
choices: Climate is a decades-long average, so two cold winters settle little
A warming world should give mild winters everywhere, so the column is right
Local weather has no connection at all to the global climate measured
Those cold winters were themselves caused by warming, so it is backwards
quiz.explain: Warming is a shift in the long-run average; year-to-year weather still varies widely around that average, so short cold spells neither confirm nor refute a trend.

quiz.prompt: Roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide people emit dissolves into the ocean instead of staying in the air. This slows the rise of atmospheric CO2. What else does it do?
quiz.answer: It makes seawater more acidic, so shells and corals form poorly
choices: It makes seawater more acidic, so shells and corals form poorly
It makes seawater saltier, so surface water sinks more readily
It releases extra oxygen, so fish populations grow more quickly
It warms the deep ocean, since the gas carries heat down with it
quiz.explain: Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, lowering ocean pH and reducing the carbonate ions that corals, molluscs and plankton need for their skeletons.

quiz.prompt: Global sea level is rising at 3.4 millimetres per year. How many centimetres does it rise over 50 years?
quiz.explain: 3.4 x 50 = 170 millimetres, which is 17 centimetres.

quiz.prompt: A country emits 500 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year and pledges a 40 percent cut. What are its emissions, in million tonnes, after the cut?
quiz.explain: A 40 percent cut leaves 60 percent: 500 x 0.6 = 300 million tonnes.

quiz.prompt: Ice cores show that at the end of past ice ages carbon dioxide rose a few centuries after temperature did. A commentator says this proves carbon dioxide cannot cause warming. Which reply is strongest?
quiz.answer: Orbital change started it; the released CO2 then amplified it
choices: The centuries-long lag is too short to be measured reliably
Orbital change started it; the released CO2 then amplified it
Past climates can tell us nothing about the present day
Carbon dioxide always follows temperature, so today is no different
quiz.explain: A trigger and an amplifier are different roles. Orbital changes started deglaciation; the carbon dioxide released then drove most of the warming that followed.

quiz.prompt: Two weather stations 50 kilometres apart show different warming trends over 40 years, and one sits in a city that has grown around it. What should a climate scientist do first?
quiz.answer: Check and adjust for local urban heating first
choices: Check and adjust for local urban heating first
Use the rural record alone, since the city one is contaminated
Average the two, since averaging cancels out local effects
Report the difference as a genuine regional climate signal
quiz.explain: Homogenisation identifies non-climatic influences such as urban growth or a moved instrument, so that what is left reflects the regional climate.

lesson_media.alt: An energy network traces sunlight to Earth's surface, infrared through greenhouse gases to space, and carbon dioxide plus water and ice feedbacks.
lesson_media.caption: The greenhouse effect is radiative energy balance, not a solid lid; climate change follows a forcing, response, and feedback chain measured in multiple records.

nodes.title: Biomes and Ecology
nodes.goal: Earth's biomes and how life shapes the planet.

quiz.prompt: Two regions lie at similar latitudes, but one is a lush rainforest and the other is a desert. The single most important difference that determines which biome forms is usually:
quiz.answer: The amount of precipitation each region receives
quiz.explain: At a given temperature range, available moisture largely determines the biome; abundant rainfall supports forests while scarcity yields deserts.
choices: The amount of precipitation each region receives
The colour and mineral content of the deeper soil
The average temperature, which differs greatly between them
The kinds of plant seeds that first reached each region

quiz.prompt: Photosynthetic life over billions of years produced most of the oxygen now in Earth's atmosphere. This is evidence that:
quiz.answer: Living things can reshape the planet's atmosphere
quiz.explain: The rise of atmospheric oxygen from photosynthesis shows the biosphere actively alters Earth's chemistry, a core idea of Earth-system ecology.
choices: Living things can reshape the planet's atmosphere
The atmosphere has held this much oxygen since Earth formed
Photosynthesis is the only process that ever changes the air
Volcanoes, not life, supplied nearly all the oxygen we breathe

quiz.prompt: In a grassland food web, a disease sharply reduces the population of wolves that prey on deer. In the short term, what is the most likely chain of effects?
quiz.answer: Deer numbers rise and heavier grazing thins the plants
quiz.explain: Removing a top predator releases its prey to increase, and larger herbivore populations then consume more vegetation, a trophic cascade.
choices: Deer numbers rise and heavier grazing thins the plants
Deer numbers rise, and the extra grazing makes the grass grow faster
Deer numbers rise briefly, then fall back as the balance restores itself
Deer numbers fall, because the disease spreads from the wolves to them

quiz.prompt: About 10 percent of the energy stored at one feeding level passes to the next. Grasses in a meadow capture 20,000 kilojoules. Rabbits eat the grass and foxes eat the rabbits. How many kilojoules reach the foxes?
quiz.explain: 20,000 x 0.1 = 2,000 kJ reaches the rabbits, and 2,000 x 0.1 = 200 kJ reaches the foxes. This steep loss is why food chains are short.

quiz.prompt: A weather station records 22 centimetres of precipitation a year, summer highs near 40 C and winter nights near freezing. Plants there have deep roots, thick waxy stems and tiny leaves. Which biome does the station sit in?
quiz.answer: Desert
choices: Desert
Tundra
Temperate grassland
Tropical rainforest
quiz.explain: Very low precipitation with large daily and seasonal temperature swings, plus water-storing plants, is the signature of a hot dry biome rather than a cold or well-watered one.

quiz.prompt: A chemical spill kills the fungi and bacteria that break down dead material in a woodland, leaving the plants and animals unharmed. What should ecologists expect over the following years?
quiz.answer: Dead matter piles up and the soil runs short of nutrients
choices: Dead matter piles up and the soil runs short of nutrients
Plants grow faster once nothing competes with them for space
Plants are unaffected, since they make their own food from air and light
The woodland carries on unchanged, since decomposers eat no living thing
quiz.explain: Decomposers return nitrogen, phosphorus and carbon from dead tissue to the soil. Remove them and the nutrient loop breaks, starving the plants that everything else depends on.

quiz.prompt: A forest stores about 150 tonnes of carbon per hectare. How many tonnes are stored across 40 hectares?
quiz.explain: 150 x 40 = 6,000 tonnes of carbon.

quiz.prompt: Deserts cover about 30 percent of Earth's 150 million square kilometres of land. How many million square kilometres is that?
quiz.explain: 30 percent of 150 million is 45 million square kilometres.

quiz.prompt: Tundra soils hold enormous amounts of undecayed plant material, far more than the soil of a tropical rainforest does. What best explains the contrast?
quiz.answer: Cold slows the decomposers, so dead matter piles up
choices: Cold slows the decomposers, so dead matter piles up
Tundra plants grow much faster than tropical ones do
The frozen ground stops roots getting down, so litter stays on top
Rainforest soil is deep, and stores its carbon far below the surface
quiz.explain: Rainforests produce more dead matter, but warmth and moisture let decomposers recycle it almost at once, so little accumulates.

quiz.prompt: A wetland upstream of a town is drained for farmland, and the town starts flooding after heavy rain. What role had the wetland played?
quiz.answer: It soaked up storm water and released it slowly
choices: It soaked up storm water and released it slowly
It dammed the river behind a wall of growing plants
It let the rain evaporate before it could reach the river
It carried the flood water away downstream more quickly
quiz.explain: Wetlands act as sponges and buffers, storing a rainfall peak and letting it out gradually instead of sending it downstream all at once.

lesson_media.alt: A biome matrix compares rainforest, grassland, desert, and tundra by temperature, water availability, and the ecological constraint shaping life.
lesson_media.caption: Climate filters which strategies persist, while organisms feed back on the physical Earth through nutrient cycling, fire, soils, and carbon storage.

nodes.title: Space Exploration
nodes.goal: Rockets, satellites and human spaceflight.

quiz.prompt: A rocket works even in the vacuum of space, where there is no air to push against. Which principle explains how it produces thrust?
quiz.answer: Exhaust thrown backward pushes the rocket forward
quiz.explain: By Newton's third law, expelling mass (exhaust) backward produces an equal forward reaction, so a rocket needs no air to push against.
choices: Exhaust thrown backward pushes the rocket forward
It pushes against the surrounding air like a swimmer
The escaping gas pushes against the launch pad below it
Burning fuel makes the rocket lighter, so it rises

quiz.prompt: A satellite in a stable low orbit is constantly pulled toward Earth by gravity, yet it never falls to the ground. Why does it stay in orbit?
quiz.answer: It moves sideways fast enough to keep missing Earth
quiz.explain: An orbit is continual free-fall: the satellite's high sideways speed means its curved fall matches Earth's curvature, so it circles rather than hitting the ground.
choices: It moves sideways fast enough to keep missing Earth
It is far too light for gravity to pull it down
Its engines fire continuously to hold it up there
Gravity does not reach as high as a satellite's orbit

quiz.prompt: Astronauts aboard the International Space Station appear to float, described as 'weightless.' The best explanation is that they are:
quiz.answer: Falling continuously around Earth with the station
quiz.explain: The ISS and its crew fall around Earth together, so astronauts float; gravity is still strong at that altitude, providing the orbit.
choices: So far from Earth that its gravity no longer reaches them
Held up by the air pressure inside the sealed cabin
Spinning with the station, which lifts them off the floor
Falling continuously around Earth with the station

quiz.prompt: A radio command travels at 300,000 kilometres per second. When Mars lies 300 million kilometres from Earth, how many minutes does the command take to reach a rover there? Round to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: 300,000,000 / 300,000 = 1,000 seconds, and 1,000 / 60 = 16.7 minutes. This lag is why rovers must drive with a good deal of their own autonomy.

quiz.prompt: A spacecraft circling Earth in a low orbit fires its engine forward along its direction of travel for a few seconds. What happens to the orbit?
quiz.answer: It swings out into a larger, higher orbit
choices: It swings out into a larger, higher orbit
It stays the same circle, but the craft travels round it faster
It rises straight away from Earth along the direction of the push
The extra speed pulls the orbit inward
quiz.explain: Adding speed adds orbital energy, so the craft climbs away from Earth on the far side of its path; counter-intuitively, its average speed over the bigger orbit ends up lower.

quiz.prompt: A returning capsule glows white-hot as it plunges into the atmosphere. Which account of that heating matches the physics?
quiz.answer: Air rammed ahead of the capsule is compressed to thousands of degrees
choices: Air rammed ahead of the capsule is compressed to thousands of degrees
Friction between the air and the capsule's skin supplies nearly all the heat
The heat shield burns as a chemical fuel once it meets the oxygen
The capsule's own speed turns directly into heat inside its metal skin
quiz.explain: At hypersonic speed the capsule cannot push air aside fast enough; a shock wave forms and violently compresses the air, and it is that superheated gas, not surface rubbing, that does most of the heating.

quiz.prompt: A rocket stage burns for 150 seconds giving an average acceleration of 20 metres per second squared. Ignoring gravity and drag losses, how many metres per second of speed does it add?
