quiz.explain: Speed added is acceleration multiplied by time: 20 x 150 = 3,000 metres per second.

quiz.prompt: The International Space Station completes one orbit every 90 minutes. How many orbits does it make in one day?
quiz.explain: A day is 1,440 minutes, and 1,440 divided by 90 is 16 orbits.

quiz.prompt: A probe bound for the outer solar system swings close past Jupiter and leaves the encounter faster than it arrived, without firing its engine. Where did the extra speed come from?
quiz.answer: From Jupiter's orbital motion, which slows a fraction
choices: From Jupiter's gravity, which pulls it in harder than it pushes it out
From Jupiter's magnetic field pushing on the probe
From Jupiter's orbital motion, which slows a fraction
Energy was created by passing so close to the planet
quiz.explain: A gravity assist is a momentum exchange with the planet. The probe gains speed relative to the Sun and Jupiter loses a truly negligible amount.

quiz.prompt: Missions to Mars can launch only during windows that come round about every 26 months. What sets that timing?
quiz.answer: The two planets must be placed for a low-energy transfer
choices: Mars comes nearest to Earth then, giving the shortest trip
The two planets must be placed for a low-energy transfer
Earth's orbit brings it closest to the Sun every 26 months
Only then does the Sun's radiation drop to a safe level
quiz.explain: A Hohmann transfer arrives where Mars will be. That geometry recurs at the synodic period of the two orbits, about 26 months.

lesson_media.alt: A mission sequence distinguishes launch thrust, sideways orbital free-fall, timed transfer burns, and the resource trade-offs of spacecraft operation.
lesson_media.caption: Spaceflight is controlled momentum and energy accounting: engines change velocity, while gravity governs the long coasting arcs between burns.

nodes.title: Geophysics & Geochemistry
nodes.goal: Earth's fields, seismology and composition.

quiz.prompt: Stations on the far side of the planet from a large earthquake record refracted P-waves but no S-waves, leaving a global shear-wave shadow. Shear waves die out in any material that cannot resist twisting. What does the shadow imply about the outer core?
quiz.answer: It behaves as a liquid, with no rigidity to carry them
choices: It behaves as a liquid, with no rigidity to carry them
It is solid iron whose crystals scatter the S-waves
It is hotter than the inner core and absorbs them
It rotates separately, deflecting the S-waves aside
quiz.explain: S-waves need a medium with rigidity; their absence across the far hemisphere, together with the sharp refraction of P-waves at the same boundary, shows the outer core is molten iron.

quiz.prompt: Earth's magnetic field is generated by motion in its liquid iron outer core (the geodynamo). A rocky planet of similar size whose core has cooled and solidified, halting this convective motion, would most likely:
quiz.answer: Have little or no global magnetic field at all
quiz.explain: A global field requires a convecting, electrically conducting fluid core; if that motion stops, the dynamo ceases and the planet loses its field, as is thought to have happened on Mars.
choices: Have little or no global magnetic field at all
Keep its field, as solid iron is magnetic
Have a stronger field than Earth's
Make its field in the atmosphere instead

quiz.prompt: Geochemists use radioactive isotopes that decay at known, constant rates to date rocks. A mineral contains a parent isotope with a half-life of 700 million years, and analysis shows it now holds one-quarter of its original parent atoms. Approximately how old is the mineral?
quiz.answer: About 1.4 billion years
quiz.explain: One-quarter remaining means two half-lives have elapsed (1/2 then 1/4), so the age is 2 x 700 million = 1.4 billion years.
choices: About 700 million years
About 2.8 billion years
About 1.4 billion years
About 350 million years

quiz.prompt: P-waves travel at 6.0 km/s and S-waves at 3.5 km/s through the crust. A seismograph records the S-wave arrival 40 seconds after the P-wave. How many kilometres from that station did the quake strike?
quiz.explain: The lag equals d/3.5 - d/6.0 = d(0.2857 - 0.1667) = 0.1190d. Setting 0.1190d = 40 gives d = 336 km; this S-P interval is how single stations estimate range.

quiz.prompt: Uranium-235 decays to lead-207 with a half-life of 704 million years. A zircon crystal now contains one uranium-235 atom for every seven lead-207 atoms produced by that decay. Give the crystal's age in millions of years.
quiz.explain: One parent per seven daughters means one eighth of the original uranium remains, so three half-lives have passed: 3 x 704 = 2,112 million years.

quiz.prompt: A survey ship tows a magnetometer back and forth across a mid-ocean ridge and records alternating bands of normal and reversed magnetisation, mirrored symmetrically about the ridge axis. Which conclusion does this pattern most directly support?
quiz.answer: Crust forms at the ridge and locks in the field as it cools
choices: Crust forms at the ridge and locks in the field as it cools
Earth's magnetic field arises in the crust rather than in the core
Magnetic minerals migrate sideways long after the lava has solidified
The ocean floor is ancient and has stayed put since it first formed
quiz.explain: Basalt freezes in the ambient field direction as it cools past the Curie point. Symmetric stripes mean crust is manufactured at the axis and carried away in both directions while the field periodically reverses.

quiz.prompt: A rock contains 12.5 percent of its original potassium-40, whose half-life is 1.25 billion years. Give the rock's age in billions of years.
quiz.explain: 12.5 percent is one-eighth, which is three half-lives: 3 x 1.25 = 3.75 billion years.

quiz.prompt: The geothermal gradient in the upper crust is 25 degrees Celsius per kilometre and the surface temperature is 10 degrees Celsius. What temperature, in degrees Celsius, is expected at 4 kilometres depth?
quiz.explain: 10 + (25 x 4) = 110 degrees Celsius.

quiz.prompt: A gravity survey across a sedimentary basin records values consistently below the regional average. Which interpretation fits best?
quiz.answer: Low-density sediments fill a deep basin there
choices: A dense body of iron ore lies beneath the survey line
Low-density sediments fill a deep basin there
The crust is unusually thin under the basin
The instrument drifted steadily during the survey
quiz.explain: A negative Bouguer anomaly means less mass than average beneath the station, which thick low-density fill supplies. Thin crust would bring dense mantle nearer the surface and raise gravity.

quiz.prompt: Seismic tomography images a fast, cold sheet of material dipping from a trench to 600 kilometres depth. Which conclusion does this best support?
quiz.answer: Subducted lithosphere sinks well down into the mantle
choices: A hot mantle plume is rising beneath that point
The crust there is unusually thick
Subducted lithosphere sinks well down into the mantle
The core-mantle boundary is shallower in that region
quiz.explain: Cold rock transmits seismic waves faster. A fast tabular anomaly descending from a trench is the sinking slab, showing subduction carries plates deep into the mantle.

lesson_media.alt: A seismogram separates earlier compressional P-wave motion from later shear S-wave motion and links S-wave absence to Earth's liquid outer core.
lesson_media.caption: Geophysics infers inaccessible interiors by combining wave travel, gravity, magnetism, and chemical constraints rather than relying on a single measurement.

nodes.title: Astrophysics
nodes.goal: The physics of stars, galaxies and radiation.

quiz.prompt: Fusing nuclei releases energy only when the product weighs less than the reactants, the missing mass appearing as energy via E=mc^2. Four hydrogen nuclei together weigh 4.0313 u; one helium-4 nucleus weighs 4.0026 u. Iron-56 has the highest binding energy per nucleon of any nucleus, so nothing fused from iron can weigh less than its reactants. Which process releases energy?
quiz.answer: Fusing hydrogen into helium, since mass is lost
quiz.explain: 4.0313 - 4.0026 = 0.0287 u is lost, and that mass becomes energy. Past iron the mass deficit reverses, so fusing iron upward costs energy rather than releasing it, and splitting helium simply undoes an energy-releasing step.
choices: Fusing hydrogen into helium, since mass is lost
Fusing iron into heavier nuclei, since iron is the most stable
Splitting helium back into hydrogen, since that frees the nucleons
Fusing any two nuclei at all, since fusion always releases energy

quiz.prompt: A star's core holds itself up against gravity with the outward push of fusion. For a very massive star at the end of its life, the core is iron and fusion can no longer release net energy. What happens next?
quiz.answer: Pressure support fails, the core implodes into a supernova
quiz.explain: Iron fusion consumes rather than releases energy, so pressure support fails, the core collapses, and the rebound drives a supernova, possibly leaving a neutron star or black hole.
choices: Iron fusion ignites and the star shines far brighter for ages
Pressure support fails, the core implodes into a supernova
The core cools into a white dwarf, as the Sun's will
The star drifts off into empty space, unchanged for ever

quiz.prompt: A black hole's event horizon is the boundary beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape. If the Sun were somehow replaced by a black hole of exactly the same mass, what would happen to Earth's orbit?
quiz.answer: Earth would keep the same orbit, since gravity depends on mass
quiz.explain: Gravitational pull at a given distance depends only on mass; with the Sun's mass unchanged, Earth's orbit stays the same (though it would go dark and cold).
choices: Earth would be pulled in at once and swallowed whole
Earth would keep the same orbit, since gravity depends on mass
Earth would spiral inward, since a black hole pulls far harder
Earth would fly free, as a black hole's pull reaches only close in

quiz.prompt: A difference of 5 magnitudes corresponds to a brightness ratio of exactly 100. How many times brighter than a magnitude 11.0 star does a magnitude 1.0 star appear?
quiz.explain: A 10-magnitude gap is two 5-magnitude steps, so the ratio is 100 x 100 = 10,000. The magnitude scale is logarithmic and runs backwards, with smaller numbers meaning brighter.

quiz.prompt: A star's luminosity follows L proportional to R squared times T to the fourth power. Star X has twice the Sun's radius and twice the Sun's surface temperature. Give Star X's luminosity as a multiple of the Sun's.
quiz.explain: Doubling the radius multiplies luminosity by 2 squared = 4, and doubling the temperature multiplies it by 2 to the fourth = 16, giving 4 x 16 = 64.

quiz.prompt: The spectrum of a distant galaxy shows the same pattern of hydrogen absorption lines seen in a laboratory lamp, but every line sits at a longer wavelength, each shifted by the same fractional amount. Which explanation accounts for the shift of the whole pattern?
quiz.answer: The galaxy recedes, stretching every wavelength by one factor
choices: The galaxy recedes, stretching every wavelength by one factor
Dust lying between us and the galaxy absorbs the shorter wavelengths
The galaxy's hydrogen is an isotope whose lines fall at other wavelengths
The galaxy's gas is far hotter, and hotter gas emits longer wavelengths
quiz.explain: Only recession multiplies every wavelength by the identical factor 1+z. Dust reddens the overall colour without moving line positions, and temperature changes line strengths rather than shifting the pattern uniformly.

quiz.prompt: Wien's law gives a blackbody's peak wavelength as 2.9 x 10^-3 metre-kelvin divided by its temperature. Give the peak wavelength, in nanometres, for a star at 12,000 K. Round to the nearest nanometre.
quiz.explain: 2.9e-3 / 12,000 = 2.417e-7 metres, which is about 242 nanometres, in the ultraviolet.

quiz.prompt: A Cepheid variable has apparent magnitude 20.0 and absolute magnitude -5.0. Using m - M = 5 log10(d/10 pc), give its distance in parsecs.
quiz.explain: m - M = 25, so log10(d/10) = 5, giving d = 10 x 10^5 = 1,000,000 parsecs.

quiz.prompt: A binary star's spectral lines split into two sets that shift back and forth with a 10-day period. What can be measured directly from that alone?
quiz.answer: Their speeds along our line of sight
choices: Their speeds along our line of sight
The individual masses of the two stars
The distance to the binary system
The surface temperature of each star
quiz.explain: Doppler shifts give radial velocities. Turning those into masses needs the orbital inclination, which spectroscopy alone does not supply.

quiz.prompt: A cluster of galaxies glows in X-rays from thin gas spread between its member galaxies. Which inference does this best support?
quiz.answer: Gravity has heated the gas to millions of degrees
choices: Gravity has heated the gas to millions of degrees
Every galaxy in the cluster hosts a bright X-ray star
The gas is falling in from outside the cluster right now
The X-rays all come from one recent supernova
quiz.explain: Gas falling into a deep gravitational potential is shock-heated to the virial temperature and radiates thermal X-rays, and this gas outweighs the stars in the galaxies.

lesson_media.alt: A Hertzsprung–Russell-style plot places the main sequence diagonally, luminous cool giants above, and hot faint white dwarfs below.
lesson_media.caption: The H–R diagram turns light measurements into a physical map where location constrains stellar radius, evolutionary state, and mass-dependent lifetime.

nodes.title: Planetary Science
nodes.goal: How worlds form and evolve.

quiz.prompt: In the solar nebula theory, planets formed from a disk of gas and dust around the young Sun. Rocky planets formed close to the Sun and gas giants farther out. Why did the giants form beyond the 'frost line'?
quiz.answer: Ices condensed there, so cores grew big enough to hold gas
quiz.explain: Past the frost line, water and other volatiles froze into solids, letting cores grow massive enough to gravitationally attract and hold thick gas envelopes.
choices: The outer planets are much older and had far more time to grow
Gas survived just in the cold outer part of the disk
The Sun pushed the heavy metals out to the outer disk
Ices condensed there, so cores grew big enough to hold gas

quiz.prompt: Astronomers detect an exoplanet by measuring the tiny, regular dip in a star's brightness every 12 days as the planet passes in front of it. This is the transit method. What can be directly inferred from a deeper dip?
quiz.answer: A larger planet compared with its host star
quiz.explain: The transit depth reflects the fraction of the star's disk the planet covers, so a bigger planet (relative to the star) causes a deeper brightness dip.
choices: A planet orbiting closer to its star
A planet made of dense metal rather than rock
A larger planet compared with its host star
A hotter planet, because it glows more brightly

quiz.prompt: A young rocky planet loses internal heat over time. Compared with a small planet, a larger planet generally stays geologically active (volcanoes, plate motion) for longer. Why?
quiz.answer: A larger body has less surface per volume, so it cools slower
quiz.explain: Heat is generated with volume but lost through surface area; larger planets have relatively less surface per volume, so they cool more slowly and stay active longer.
choices: A larger body has less surface per volume, so it cools slower
Bigger planets have thick atmospheres that trap their internal heat
Smaller planets have thinner crusts, so heat escapes at once
Larger planets sit closer to the Sun and stay warmer inside

quiz.prompt: For a planet orbiting a one-solar-mass star, Kepler's third law reads P squared equals a cubed, with P in years and a in astronomical units. An exoplanet orbits such a star at 4 AU. Give its orbital period in years.
quiz.explain: a cubed = 4 x 4 x 4 = 64, so P = the square root of 64 = 8 years.

quiz.prompt: A resonance with Europa and Ganymede holds Io on a slightly elliptical orbit, so Jupiter's tidal bulge on Io rises and falls once per orbit. That constant kneading dissipates enough frictional heat to drive hundreds of volcanoes on a body smaller than Earth's geologically dead Moon. Suppose the resonance were broken and Io settled onto a perfectly circular orbit at the same average distance. What should happen to the volcanism?
quiz.answer: It would fade away, since the tidal flexing would stop
choices: It would fade away, since the tidal flexing would stop
It would intensify on a closer circular orbit
It would continue, powered by radioactive rock
It would continue, since the tidal pull remains
quiz.explain: Heating comes from the bulge changing, not from the bulge existing. On a circular orbit the tidal distortion is steady, so nothing is kneaded and no frictional heat is produced; Io is far too small for radioactivity alone to keep it molten.

quiz.prompt: Two moons of equal size orbit one planet. Moon A's surface swarms with overlapping craters; Moon B shows barely a dozen. Which inference about Moon B does this best support?
quiz.answer: Something resurfaced it after the era of heavy bombardment
choices: Something resurfaced it after the era of heavy bombardment
It formed long after Moon A and so met far fewer impacts
Its weaker gravity draws in far fewer of the passing impactors
Moon A screens it from most objects entering the planet's space
quiz.explain: Impactors rained on both moons alike, so crater density measures surface age. A sparsely cratered surface has been renewed by volcanism, tectonics or icy flow since the bombardment.

quiz.prompt: For a planet orbiting a one-solar-mass star, P squared equals a cubed with P in years and a in astronomical units. A planet has a period of 27 years. Give its orbital radius in astronomical units.
quiz.explain: 27 squared is 729, so a cubed is 729 and a is 9 astronomical units.

quiz.prompt: A transit dims a star by 1 percent. The planet's radius divided by the star's radius equals the square root of the transit depth. Give that ratio.
quiz.explain: The square root of 0.01 is 0.1, so the planet is one-tenth the star's radius.

quiz.prompt: Mars and Venus are broadly similar in size, yet Mars retains only a wisp of atmosphere. Beyond distance from the Sun, which factor best explains the loss?
quiz.answer: Weaker gravity and no global magnetic field let the gas escape
choices: A giant impact blew most of the atmosphere away in one event
Weaker gravity and no global magnetic field let the gas escape
Mars spins so slowly that its air collects on the night side
Dust storms lifted the gas high enough for the Sun to burn it off
quiz.explain: Mars has roughly a tenth of Earth's mass and lost its dynamo early, so the solar wind has been able to strip the upper atmosphere for billions of years.

quiz.prompt: A moon orbiting close to a giant planet has a surface of long parallel ridges and almost no impact craters. What is the most reasonable inference?
quiz.answer: Tidal heating keeps its surface young
choices: Tidal heating keeps its surface young
It was recently captured
An atmosphere has slowly erased the surface craters
Its ice is soft enough that craters slump away on their own
quiz.explain: Few craters means a young surface, and a small body near a giant planet has an obvious internal heat source in tidal flexing.

lesson_media.alt: A planet-formation sequence moves from a temperature-structured disk through accretion and impact heating to differentiation and long-term geological evolution.
lesson_media.caption: Worlds inherit starting materials from disks, then diverge through mass-dependent heat retention, atmospheric escape, impacts, and internal activity.

nodes.title: Climatology
nodes.goal: Climate models and the carbon budget.

quiz.prompt: Climate scientists run global circulation models twice: once with only natural factors (solar changes, volcanoes) and once adding human greenhouse-gas emissions. Only the second run reproduces the observed warming since 1950. This attribution study supports which conclusion?
quiz.answer: Human emissions are the dominant cause of recent warming
quiz.explain: When only the human-forcing run matches observations, it attributes the warming primarily to anthropogenic greenhouse gases.
choices: Human emissions are the dominant cause of recent warming
Natural factors explain the warming just as well as humans do
The models were tuned to match, so the test proves nothing
Human emissions and natural causes contribute about equally

quiz.prompt: The idea of a 'carbon budget' is the total additional CO2 that can be emitted while keeping warming below a target like 1.5C. If annual emissions stay high, the main implication for the budget is that:
quiz.answer: The remaining budget runs out sooner, requiring faster cuts
quiz.explain: A fixed cumulative budget depletes faster at higher emission rates, leaving less time and demanding steeper reductions to meet the target.
choices: The remaining budget runs out sooner, requiring faster cuts
Reaching zero later would still bring the temperature back to target
The budget refills as oceans and forests take carbon up
Warming depends on the yearly rate, not the total

quiz.prompt: A general circulation model divides the atmosphere and ocean into a 3D grid and steps forward in time using physical equations. A modeler wants finer detail over a mountainous region. The main trade-off of using a much finer grid is that it:
quiz.answer: Improves spatial detail but greatly raises computing cost
quiz.explain: Finer resolution captures smaller features but multiplies the number of grid cells and calculations, sharply raising computational cost.
choices: Improves spatial detail but greatly raises computing cost
Makes the model run faster, since each grid cell is smaller
Removes the need to approximate clouds and convection at all
Improves the detail but makes the long-range projection less reliable

quiz.prompt: A model has an equilibrium climate sensitivity of 3.0 C per doubling of carbon dioxide. Starting from the pre-industrial 280 parts per million, how much equilibrium warming, in degrees Celsius, does the model give at 1,120 parts per million?
quiz.explain: 1,120 / 280 = 4, which is two doublings, so the warming is 2 x 3.0 = 6.0 C. Forcing rises with the logarithm of concentration, so equal warming needs each doubling, not each fixed increment.

quiz.prompt: Global average temperature fell about 0.5 C for roughly two years after the 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo, then climbed back to trend. Which mechanism best accounts for that pattern?
quiz.answer: Sulfate droplets above the weather layer reflected sunlight
choices: Sulfate droplets above the weather layer reflected sunlight
Ash in the lower air shaded the surface until rain washed it out
Sulfur dioxide gas itself absorbed the incoming sunlight
Ozone destroyed by the eruption let more heat escape to space
quiz.explain: Sulfur dioxide injected above the weather layer converts to reflective sulfate droplets that linger a year or two because no rain reaches them; tropospheric ash rains out within weeks and cannot cool the planet for years.

quiz.prompt: A model run in 1990 projected 2020 global temperature to within about 0.1 C. A critic answers that weather forecasts fail beyond ten days, so a thirty-year projection deserves no trust. Which reply best answers the critic?
quiz.answer: Long-run statistics stay predictable when daily states do not
choices: Long-run statistics stay predictable when daily states do not
The same equations bind both, so the same limit applies
Weather forecasts fail only from their coarser grids
The 1990 agreement was luck, not physics
quiz.explain: Weather forecasting is an initial-value problem wrecked by chaos; climate projection is a boundary-value problem, asking what the statistics settle to under a given forcing, which stays tractable.

quiz.prompt: Doubling carbon dioxide gives a radiative forcing of 3.7 watts per square metre, and a model's climate sensitivity parameter is 0.8 degrees Celsius per watt per square metre. Give the equilibrium warming in degrees Celsius, to two decimal places.
quiz.explain: 3.7 x 0.8 = 2.96 degrees Celsius of equilibrium warming.

quiz.prompt: Global emissions run at 40 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide a year, and the remaining budget for 1.5 degrees is 400 gigatonnes. At constant emissions, how many years until the budget is exhausted?
quiz.explain: 400 divided by 40 is 10 years.

quiz.prompt: Models disagree widely about future rainfall in one region but agree closely on its warming. What should a planner take from this?
quiz.answer: Plan around the agreed warming; treat rainfall as uncertain
choices: Plan around the agreed warming; treat rainfall as uncertain
Wait for the models to agree on warming before planning
Average the rainfall runs and treat the result as settled
Adopt the wettest model, as the safest possible case
quiz.explain: Model spread is information. Where projections converge the signal is robust; where they diverge, plans should be built to work across the range.

quiz.prompt: Ocean heat content rose steadily through a decade in which surface air temperature rose much more slowly. Which reading is best supported?
quiz.answer: Energy kept accumulating, with more of it going into the ocean
choices: The ocean warmed the air, so the surface record must read too low
Energy kept accumulating, with more of it going into the ocean
The planet's energy imbalance paused during that decade
Warming stopped; the ocean reading means something else
quiz.explain: The ocean holds the overwhelming majority of the extra heat. Surface temperature is a noisy indicator because heat can be shifted between reservoirs.

lesson_media.alt: A central near-linear warming-versus-cumulative-carbon curve lies between explicit lower and upper response bounds, explaining why a chosen temperature limit implies an uncertain finite carbon budget.
lesson_media.caption: Climate models combine physical conservation laws with observations; ensembles quantify scenario and parameter uncertainty rather than eliminating it.

nodes.title: Ocean & Atmospheric Science
nodes.goal: Fluid dynamics of air and sea.

quiz.prompt: Because Earth rotates, large-scale moving air and water are deflected (the Coriolis effect): to the right in the Northern Hemisphere. Around a low-pressure center in the Northern Hemisphere, air spiraling inward is therefore turned so that the winds rotate:
quiz.answer: Counterclockwise
quiz.explain: Air rushing toward a Northern-Hemisphere low is deflected to the right, producing a counterclockwise (cyclonic) circulation.
choices: Counterclockwise
Clockwise
Straight inward with no turning at all
Counterclockwise near the pole, clockwise near the equator

quiz.prompt: In physical oceanography, the deep 'thermohaline' circulation is driven by differences in water density. Which change would make surface seawater denser and prone to sinking, helping drive this circulation?
quiz.answer: Becoming colder and saltier
quiz.explain: Cold, salty water is denser than warm or fresh water, so it sinks, driving the deep overturning (thermohaline) circulation.
choices: Becoming colder and saltier
Becoming warmer and fresher
Becoming warmer and slightly saltier
Absorbing more sunlight at the surface

quiz.prompt: A flow's Reynolds number is its speed multiplied by the channel width and divided by the fluid's viscosity; the flow turns turbulent above a critical value. An engineer must double the speed of coolant through a channel while leaving the Reynolds number, and so the smooth laminar flow, exactly as it was. Which single change does that?
quiz.answer: Halve the channel's width
quiz.explain: Re is proportional to speed times width divided by viscosity. Doubling the speed and halving the width leaves the product unchanged. Doubling the width or halving the viscosity would each multiply Re by four, and the channel's length does not enter the formula at all.
choices: Halve the channel's width
Double the channel's width
Halve the coolant's viscosity
Make the channel twice as long

quiz.prompt: A tsunami crosses the deep ocean as a shallow-water wave, with speed equal to the square root of g times d, where g is 9.8 m/s squared and d is the water depth. Over an abyssal plain 4,000 metres deep, what is its speed in metres per second? Round to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: 9.8 x 4,000 = 39,200, and the square root of 39,200 is about 198 m/s, roughly 710 km/h, which is why deep-ocean tsunamis cross a basin in hours.

quiz.prompt: Steady winds blow parallel to a north-south coastline in the Northern Hemisphere, and the surface layer drifts 90 degrees to the right of the wind, away from the shore. That coast supports one of the world's richest fisheries. Which consequence explains the catch?
quiz.answer: Cold, nutrient-rich water wells up from below
choices: Cold, nutrient-rich water wells up from below
Warm tropical water piles against the shore
Sinking water carries oxygen down to the fish
Trapped river water fertilises the surface
quiz.explain: Offshore Ekman transport must be replaced from beneath, drawing up water charged with nitrate and phosphate from the dark deep ocean and igniting the phytoplankton bloom that the fishery feeds on.

quiz.prompt: A parcel of unsaturated air at the same temperature as its surroundings is nudged upward one kilometre. It cools at the dry adiabatic rate of 10 C per kilometre; the surrounding air cools with height at 6 C per kilometre. Predict what the parcel does next.
quiz.answer: It sinks back, colder and denser than the air around it
choices: It sinks back, colder and denser than the air around it
It keeps rising, since it stays warmer than its surroundings
It accelerates upward and builds into a towering thunderstorm
It hovers at the new height, matching the surrounding temperature
quiz.explain: After one kilometre the parcel is 10 C cooler while the environment is only 6 C cooler, so the parcel sits 4 C colder and denser and returns. An environmental lapse rate below the adiabatic rate means a stable atmosphere.

quiz.prompt: Seawater density is 1,025 kilograms per cubic metre and g is 9.8 metres per second squared. What pressure, in kilopascals, does the water alone exert at 200 metres depth?
quiz.explain: 1,025 x 9.8 x 200 = 2,009,000 pascals, which is 2,009 kilopascals.

quiz.prompt: A deep-water wave's speed in metres per second is about 1.25 times the square root of its wavelength in metres. Give the speed for a wavelength of 64 metres.
quiz.explain: The square root of 64 is 8, and 1.25 x 8 = 10 metres per second.

quiz.prompt: A coastal town gets a breeze off the sea each afternoon and a breeze off the land overnight, because land changes temperature far faster than water does: whichever surface is warmer has air rising over it, and the surface flow runs in to replace that air. One cold, dull winter week the sea stays warmer than the land right through the day. Predict the afternoon breeze that week.
quiz.answer: It reverses, blowing from land out to sea by day
choices: It reverses, blowing from land out to sea by day
It strengthens, since the temperature gap is larger
It stops entirely, since breezes need summer heating
It keeps its usual direction but arrives later in the day
quiz.explain: The breeze always blows toward the warmer surface. With the sea warmer all day, air rises over the water and the afternoon flow runs from land to sea, which is the direction that normally belongs to the night.

quiz.prompt: During a strong El Nino the Pacific trade winds slacken and warm surface water piles up in the east. What follows for the eastern Pacific fishery?
quiz.answer: Upwelling weakens, and the catches fall away
choices: Upwelling weakens, and the catches fall away
Upwelling strengthens and catches rise
The fish simply follow the warm water
The catch shifts west with the cold water
quiz.explain: The deep warm layer blocks cold nutrient-rich water from reaching the surface, so productivity collapses and the anchovy fishery with it.

lesson_media.alt: A rotating-fluid network links unequal heating to pressure gradients and winds, then labels ideal depth-integrated Ekman transport as right of the wind in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern Hemisphere before coastal upwelling.
lesson_media.caption: Ekman transport is an idealised, hemispherically signed result of wind stress, rotation, and friction; boundaries and stratification shape the observed air–sea circulation.

nodes.title: Cosmology
nodes.goal: The universe's origin, structure and fate.

quiz.prompt: Observations show that distant galaxies are receding from us, and more distant galaxies recede faster (Hubble's law). Run backward in time, this expansion implies that:
quiz.answer: The universe was smaller, denser, and hotter in the past
quiz.explain: Uniform expansion extrapolated backward means everything was once compressed into a hot, dense state, the basis of Big Bang cosmology.
choices: The galaxies have held their present distances since forming
The universe was smaller, denser, and hotter in the past
Earth sits at the exact centre of a static universe
Galaxies fly apart through a space that was always this size

quiz.prompt: The cosmic microwave background is relic light released when the universe first cooled enough for atoms to form, and cosmic expansion has stretched its wavelength ever since. Because that stretching is what cools it, its temperature is inversely proportional to the size of the universe. It measures 2.7 K today. What would an observer have measured back when the universe was half its present size?
quiz.answer: A blackbody at roughly 5.4 K
quiz.explain: Temperature scales as one over the scale factor, so halving the size doubles it: 2.7 x 2 = 5.4 K. The background was released long before the universe reached half its present size, so it was certainly there to be measured.
choices: A blackbody at roughly 5.4 K
A blackbody at roughly 1.4 K
The same 2.7 K, since it is a fixed constant of nature
Nothing at all, since the background had not yet been released

quiz.prompt: Distant supernovae turn out fainter than a steadily decelerating universe predicts, implying the expansion has sped up. What role does dark energy play in accounting for that?
quiz.answer: Provide a repulsive push that accelerates cosmic expansion
quiz.explain: Dark energy acts like a pervasive negative pressure that overcomes gravity's attraction and accelerates cosmic expansion.
choices: Gradually slow light down over vast cosmic distances
Add extra hidden gravity that pulls galaxies together faster
Provide a repulsive push that accelerates cosmic expansion
Slow the expansion, making distant supernovae look fainter

quiz.prompt: Take the Hubble constant as 70 km/s per megaparsec. A galaxy's spectrum gives a recession velocity of 21,000 km/s. How many megaparsecs away does Hubble's law place it?
quiz.explain: Distance = velocity / H0 = 21,000 / 70 = 300 megaparsecs. Beyond the local group, redshift becomes the workhorse distance indicator.

quiz.prompt: Light from a quasar set out when the universe stood at one fifth of its present size. Using 1 + z = 1/a, with a for the scale factor at emission, compute the redshift we now measure.
quiz.explain: With a = 0.2, 1 + z = 1/0.2 = 5, so z = 4. Redshift is a direct readout of how much the universe has expanded since the light set out.

quiz.prompt: The cosmic microwave background varies in temperature by only a few parts in 100,000 across the sky, yet matter today clumps into galaxies and vast filaments. What role do those faint fluctuations play in that story?
quiz.answer: They map density seeds that gravity later grew into galaxies
choices: They map density seeds that gravity later grew into galaxies
They record light emitted by the first galaxies as they switched on
They mark where dark energy pushed matter apart most forcefully
They come from foreground dust and carry no cosmological signal
quiz.explain: The anisotropies are slight over- and under-densities at recombination. Gravity worked on them for 13 billion years, growing tiny contrasts into the cosmic web, which is why their measured spectrum constrains cosmological parameters so tightly.

quiz.prompt: A spectral line measured at 400 nanometres in the laboratory is observed at 500 nanometres in a distant galaxy. Give the redshift z.
Take the Hubble constant as 70 km/s per megaparsec, with 1 megaparsec = 3.09 x 10^19 km and 1 year = 3.15 x 10^7 s. Give the Hubble time in billions of years, to the nearest billion.
quiz.explain: 1/H0 = 3.09e19 / 70 = 4.41e17 s. Dividing by 3.15e7 s per year gives about 1.4e10 years, or 14 billion years.

quiz.prompt: A deep survey counts faint galaxies across the whole sky and finds the same number density everywhere to within a fraction of a percent, however far out it looks. Which assumption does this most directly support?
quiz.answer: On large scales the universe looks the same in every direction
choices: On large scales the universe looks the same in every direction
Earth must occupy a position at the very centre of the universe
The expansion has come to a halt at the very greatest distances
The universe must therefore be finite rather than infinite in extent
quiz.explain: This is observed isotropy. Combined with the assumption that we are not special observers, it gives the homogeneity underpinning standard cosmology.

quiz.prompt: Fitting the microwave background gives one value for today's expansion rate; nearby supernovae give a value about 8 percent higher, and both have small stated uncertainties. What is the most careful statement?
quiz.answer: Either an unrecognised systematic or new physics is at work
choices: The two methods measure different epochs, so both can be right
Either an unrecognised systematic or new physics is at work
An 8 percent gap is small enough to be ordinary scatter
The universe expands at two different rates at once
quiz.explain: The Hubble tension is a genuine disagreement between an early-universe inference and a late-universe measurement, and either could be resolved by systematics or by new physics.

lesson_media.alt: An explicitly not-to-time-scale cosmic timeline orders the hot early universe, first-minutes nucleosynthesis, cosmic microwave background release, galaxy growth, late accelerated expansion, and the present at 13.8 billion years.
lesson_media.caption: The compressed positions show sequence only: Big Bang cosmology describes expansion from a hot dense state, not an explosion from one location into pre-existing empty space.

nodes.title: Astrobiology
nodes.goal: The search for life beyond Earth.

quiz.prompt: The 'habitable zone' around a star is the range of orbital distances where a planet could have liquid water on its surface. A star much more luminous than the Sun would have its habitable zone located:
quiz.answer: Farther out from the star than the Sun's habitable zone
quiz.explain: A brighter star delivers more energy, so the region warm enough (but not too hot) for liquid water lies at greater distances.
choices: Farther out from the star than the Sun's habitable zone
Spread over a much narrower band than the Sun's zone
At exactly the same distance as the Sun's habitable zone
Much closer in to the star than the Sun's habitable zone

quiz.prompt: Astrobiologists often search for biosignatures such as an atmosphere rich in both oxygen and methane, which react with each other and would vanish without continual replenishment. Why is this combination considered a promising sign of life?
quiz.answer: Their coexistence implies something keeps producing them
quiz.explain: Oxygen and methane destroy each other chemically, so finding both in equilibrium implies active replenishment, a plausible sign of life (though not proof).
choices: Both gases are made only by living organisms on Earth
Their coexistence implies something keeps producing them
Their presence proves the planet already carries life
Both gases are rare, so finding either one is remarkable

quiz.prompt: A SETI pipeline discards broadband bursts but flags anything confined to a few hertz. Why is the narrow band the interesting case?
quiz.answer: Natural sources rarely make them, hinting at technology
quiz.explain: Most cosmic radio emission is broadband; a persistent narrow-band signal would be difficult to explain naturally and could point to a technological origin.
choices: Natural sources rarely make them, hinting at technology
Narrow-band signals carry far more information than broad ones
Narrow-band signals travel further before they fade away
Only narrow-band signals can cross interstellar dust clouds

quiz.prompt: The Drake equation multiplies R* x fp x ne x fl x fi x fc x L. Take R* = 2 per year, fp = 1, ne = 0.5, fl = 0.1, fi = 0.01, fc = 0.5 and L = 10,000 years. What value of N does this give?
quiz.explain: 2 x 1 x 0.5 x 0.1 x 0.01 x 0.5 = 0.0005 civilisations arising per year; multiplied by a 10,000-year lifetime that leaves 5 detectable at once. The result swings by orders of magnitude on the poorly known factors.

quiz.prompt: Cassini flew through the plumes venting from cracks near Enceladus's south pole and measured water vapour, sodium salts, silica nanograins and molecular hydrogen. Which inference about the moon's subsurface ocean do these measurements most strongly support?
quiz.answer: Hot water is reacting with rock on the ocean floor
choices: Hot water is reacting with rock on the ocean floor
The plume comes from Saturn's rings, not the moon
Sunlight drives photosynthesis under the ice
Organisms have already been found in the ocean
quiz.explain: Silica nanograins and molecular hydrogen form where water above roughly 90 C attacks rock, so the ocean touches a warm rocky floor, and that hydrogen offers exactly the redox couple some Earth microbes live on.

quiz.prompt: A team detects abundant methane in the atmosphere of a rocky exoplanet and announces it as a possible biosignature. Which further finding would most weaken the biological interpretation?
quiz.answer: Serpentinising rock there makes methane without any life
choices: The atmosphere also holds a large amount of carbon dioxide
Serpentinising rock there makes methane without any life
The host star flares often, destroying methane fast
The planet's mass turns out to be smaller than Earth's
quiz.explain: A biosignature only counts if abiotic routes are excluded. Serpentinisation of ultramafic rock makes methane geologically; frequent flaring would strengthen the case by demanding rapid replenishment.

quiz.prompt: A spectrograph collects 3 photons an hour from a faint target. How many hours of observation are needed to collect 240 photons?
quiz.explain: 240 divided by 3 is 80 hours.

quiz.prompt: Using N = R* x fp x ne x fl x fi x fc x L with R* = 3 per year, fp = 0.5, ne = 2, fl = 0.5, fi = 0.02, fc = 0.2 and L = 5,000 years, give N.
Microbes are found thriving three kilometres down in solid rock, living on hydrogen released when water reacts with minerals. What is the strongest implication for the search for life elsewhere?
quiz.answer: A world can host life with no sunlit surface at all
choices: A world can host life with no sunlit surface at all
Life on Mars must therefore already exist
Any planet with rock and water must already hold life
Only deep subsurface life can survive on other planets
quiz.explain: Chemosynthetic subsurface ecosystems widen the target list to icy moons and to Mars, where any surviving biosphere would most plausibly be underground.

quiz.prompt: A rocky exoplanet orbiting an active M dwarf shows abundant oxygen in its atmosphere and nothing else out of chemical equilibrium. Which caution matters most?
quiz.answer: Ultraviolet can split water and build oxygen without life
choices: Ultraviolet can split water and build oxygen without life
Oxygen cannot accumulate at all unless photosynthesis makes it
M dwarf flares would destroy the oxygen before it could build up
Oxygen is too reactive to be detected in a distant atmosphere
quiz.explain: Photolysis of water followed by hydrogen escape is a well-modelled abiotic route to oxygen, which is why a single gas is a weak biosignature.

lesson_media.alt: An astrobiology evidence tree separates potentially habitable conditions from a contextual biosignature and the multiple tests required for confirmation.
lesson_media.caption: Life detection is an inference problem: credible claims must outperform abiotic explanations and survive instrument, stellar, geological, and contamination checks.

nodes.title: Earth System Science
nodes.goal: The planet as one coupled system.

quiz.prompt: Earth-system science treats atmosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere and geosphere as one coupled system. Two solubility facts do much of the coupling work: warmer seawater holds less dissolved carbon dioxide, and warmer seawater also holds less dissolved oxygen. A model warms the ocean surface by 2 degrees Celsius. Which pair of consequences follows?
quiz.answer: More CO2 moves into the air, and sea animals have less oxygen
quiz.explain: Both gases come out of solution as the water warms. The carbon dioxide it can no longer hold outgasses to the atmosphere, adding to the warming, while the oxygen it can no longer hold leaves less for marine life. One temperature change therefore reaches the atmosphere and the biosphere at once.
choices: More CO2 moves into the air, and sea animals have less oxygen
Less CO2 moves into the air, and sea animals have more oxygen
More CO2 moves into the air, and sea animals have more oxygen
Less CO2 moves into the air, and sea animals have less oxygen

quiz.prompt: Supporters of a self-regulating Earth point to one long-run fact about the planet's surface conditions over billions of years. Which observation do they cite?
quiz.answer: Earth stayed habitable even as the Sun grew much brighter
quiz.explain: Despite the Sun growing ~30% brighter over geologic time, biologically mediated feedbacks (e.g., on CO2) have helped keep Earth habitable, a key Gaian argument.
choices: The Sun's output has stayed constant over Earth's history
Earth's climate has swung wildly with little stability
Earth stayed habitable even as the Sun grew much brighter
Earth's temperature has never varied by more than a degree

quiz.prompt: Over millions of years, silicate rock weathering consumes atmospheric CO2, and the weathering rate rises when the climate is warmer and wetter. This makes it a negative, stabilising feedback on the carbon cycle. Now suppose a long burst of volcanism doubles the CO2 in the air. Applying that feedback, what does it predict for the following few million years?
quiz.answer: Warming speeds weathering, which draws the extra CO2 back down
quiz.explain: A negative feedback opposes the change that drove it. Extra CO2 warms and moistens the climate, faster weathering then consumes CO2 more quickly than before, and the excess is drawn down until the system settles again. This is the thermostat that has kept Earth habitable across geological time.
choices: Warming speeds weathering, which draws the extra CO2 back down
Warming slows weathering, so the extra CO2 simply stays in the air
Weathering is unchanged, so CO2 falls only once volcanism stops
Warming speeds weathering, which releases still more CO2

quiz.prompt: The atmosphere holds about 750 gigatonnes of carbon, and about 210 gigatonnes leaves it each year into oceans and vegetation. What is the mean residence time of a carbon atom in the atmosphere, in years? Round to one decimal place.
quiz.explain: Residence time = reservoir / flux = 750 / 210 = 3.6 years. This measures how fast atoms swap, not how long an added pulse of CO2 perturbs the system.

quiz.prompt: A single CO2 molecule leaves the atmosphere within a few years, yet a pulse of emitted CO2 keeps warming the climate for centuries. Explain how both statements can be true.
quiz.answer: Individual molecules exchange rapidly with the ocean surface and the biosphere, so the residence time of one molecule is short, but that exchange is a two-way swap that returns as much carbon as it takes. Removing the extra carbon depends on much slower sinks such as deep-ocean mixing and rock weathering, so the added burden persists for centuries.
quiz.explain: Residence time and perturbation lifetime are different quantities: fast two-way exchange does not shrink the excess inventory, which only slow sinks can draw down.

quiz.prompt: A coupled model slowly adds freshwater to the North Atlantic; the overturning circulation weakens, then shuts down. When the modellers slowly remove that freshwater again, the circulation does not restart at the threshold where it collapsed. The system shows hysteresis: its state depends on the path taken, not on the present forcing alone. A policy team asks what that implies if a real collapse ever happened.
quiz.answer: Restoring today's conditions might not restore the circulation
choices: Restoring today's conditions might not restore the circulation
The collapse could be undone by reversing the forcing
The circulation would restart once the forcing stopped rising
The threshold is the same in both directions
quiz.explain: Two stable states exist over a range of forcing, so the system follows one branch on the way down and a different one on the way back. Undoing the forcing is therefore no guarantee of undoing the collapse, and the recovery threshold sits well past the collapse threshold.

quiz.prompt: A lake holds 60 million cubic metres of water, and rivers deliver 15 million cubic metres a year. Give the mean residence time in years.
quiz.explain: Residence time is the stock divided by the flux: 60 / 15 = 4 years.

quiz.prompt: Earth intercepts 1,361 watts per square metre of sunlight and reflects 30 percent. Averaged over the globe the absorbed flux is (1 - albedo) times the solar constant, divided by 4. Give the absorbed flux in watts per square metre, to the nearest whole number.
quiz.explain: 1,361 x 0.7 = 952.7, and 952.7 / 4 = 238 watts per square metre.

quiz.prompt: Thawing permafrost releases methane, which warms the climate, which thaws more permafrost. A modeller must decide if this runs away. Which quantity settles it?
quiz.answer: Whether the loop gain is below or above one
choices: Whether the loop gain is below or above one
How potent methane is per molecule
How much methane the permafrost holds in total
How cold the permafrost was before the thaw began
quiz.explain: A reinforcing feedback with a gain below one converges on a finite amplified response; only a gain of one or more gives runaway behaviour.

quiz.prompt: Phosphorus, unlike carbon and nitrogen, has no significant gaseous form. Which consequence for its cycle follows?
quiz.answer: It moves through rock, water and sediment, not through air
choices: It moves through rock, water and sediment, not through air
It cycles faster than carbon, since rock releases it steadily
It is evenly available worldwide, since rock is everywhere
Its losses to the deep sea are quickly returned by rainfall
quiz.explain: With no atmospheric reservoir, phosphorus moves slowly from rock to soil to sea to sediment, and is often the nutrient that runs out first in freshwater systems.

lesson_media.alt: A four-row Earth-system matrix separates atmosphere–ocean and land–biosphere exchanges, the cryosphere's sunlight reflection to space, and human greenhouse and land-use forcing.
lesson_media.caption: The stock–flux–effect columns distinguish material exchange from radiative feedback: less ice lowers albedo, increases absorbed sunlight, and amplifies warming.

nodes.title: Cosmic Frontiers
nodes.goal: Gravitational waves, dark matter and open questions.

quiz.prompt: Two instruments record a millisecond stretch-then-squeeze of their multi-kilometre arms, with nothing arriving in any telescope at that instant. In general relativity, what passed through them?
quiz.answer: Ripples in spacetime made by accelerating masses
quiz.explain: Gravitational waves are distortions of spacetime radiated by violently accelerating masses. The other three are the real vetoes an observatory must clear: radio and neutrino bursts leave the arms alone, and seismic tremors do not arrive at two continents within the light-travel time.
choices: Ripples in spacetime made by accelerating masses
A burst of radio waves from a distant magnetar
Ground vibration from a far-off earthquake
A pulse of neutrinos passing through the detectors

quiz.prompt: Dark matter is inferred because a galaxy's outer stars orbit faster than the visible matter's gravity can explain. For a star at radius r, the orbital speed v obeys v squared = G times M(<r) divided by r, where M(<r) is all the mass inside that orbit. Measured rotation curves are flat: v barely changes out well beyond the edge of the visible disc. What must M(<r) be doing out there?
quiz.answer: Growing in proportion to r
quiz.explain: If v is constant then M(<r) = v squared times r divided by G, so the enclosed mass must keep rising in step with radius. Visible matter stops, so something unseen must go on adding mass out into a halo well past the light.
choices: Growing in proportion to r
Staying constant once the starlight runs out
Falling off as one over r
Growing as r squared

quiz.prompt: A theorist presents a multiverse model that reproduces our physics exactly but makes no prediction distinguishable from within our own universe. What is the central scientific objection?
quiz.answer: Other universes may be impossible to test or observe
quiz.explain: If other universes cannot be observed even in principle, the idea is hard to test empirically, raising concerns about its scientific status.
choices: Other universes may be impossible to test or observe
It contradicts the observed expansion of our universe
It requires abandoning much of our known physics
It cannot explain why our universe has the physics it does

quiz.prompt: LIGO's arms are 4 kilometres long. A passing gravitational wave changes each arm's length by a fraction h = 1 x 10^-21 of that length. Express the length change in units of 10^-18 metres.
quiz.explain: 4,000 m x 1 x 10^-21 = 4 x 10^-18 m, about a thousandth the width of a proton, which is why the interferometer needs such extreme isolation.

quiz.prompt: Two detectors 3,000 km apart register matching signals 7 milliseconds apart, each sweeping upward from 35 Hz to 250 Hz in under a second before cutting off. Which conclusion do those two features best support?
quiz.answer: A compact binary spiralled together, and the delay narrows its position
choices: A compact binary spiralled together, and the delay narrows its position
A local seismic tremor shook both sites within a few milliseconds
A pulsar spun down, sounding a steady tone at both detectors
A supernova exploded, and both detectors imaged its light
quiz.explain: A rising chirp is the signature of an inspiral whose orbit tightens and quickens until merger, and a delay under the 10 ms light-travel time between sites confirms a real astrophysical wavefront while triangulating its direction.

quiz.prompt: In the Bullet Cluster, X-ray maps place the hot gas, which carries most of the ordinary matter, stalled between two colliding groups, while gravitational lensing places most of the mass out with the galaxies on either side. Which position does that separation most challenge?
quiz.answer: Modified-gravity models in which gravity follows the visible matter
choices: Modified-gravity models in which gravity follows the visible matter
The view that lensing traces total mass along the line of sight
The claim that dark matter passes through itself almost freely
The finding that clusters hold hot X-ray-emitting gas
quiz.explain: If gravity simply tracked luminous matter, the lensing mass would sit with the gas, since the gas outweighs the stars. Its separation from the mass peaks is the cleanest empirical case for a collisionless dark component.

quiz.prompt: Two gravitational-wave detectors sit 3,000 kilometres apart and the signal travels at 300,000 kilometres per second. What is the largest possible arrival-time difference between them, in milliseconds?
quiz.explain: 3,000 / 300,000 = 0.01 seconds, which is 10 milliseconds, for a source lying along the line joining them.

quiz.prompt: A galaxy cluster's total mass from lensing is 1.2 x 10^15 solar masses, while its stars and hot gas together come to 1.8 x 10^14. What percentage of the mass is in neither stars nor gas?
quiz.explain: The unaccounted mass is 1.2e15 - 1.8e14 = 1.02e15, and 1.02e15 / 1.2e15 = 0.85, or 85 percent.

quiz.prompt: A dark matter detector reports an excess of events whose rate varies with a one-year period. Before any discovery claim, which check matters most?
quiz.answer: Whether known backgrounds also vary through the year
choices: Whether known backgrounds also vary through the year
Whether the detector sits deep enough underground
Whether dark matter is a particle at all
Whether other experiments use the same target material
quiz.explain: An annual modulation is expected from Earth's motion through the halo, but muon flux, radon and temperature also cycle annually, so those must be excluded first.

quiz.prompt: A modified-gravity theory is tuned until it reproduces galaxy rotation curves. Which further test would bear on it most sharply?
quiz.answer: Whether it also fits clusters and the microwave background
choices: Whether it also fits clusters and the microwave background
Whether it can be written down in a simpler mathematical form
Whether it reproduces those very same rotation curves again
Whether it needs fewer free parameters than dark matter does
quiz.explain: A theory fitted to one dataset earns nothing from refitting it. The test is out-of-sample: independent systems on quite different scales.

lesson_media.alt: A cosmic-frontier matrix separates direct observations, supported physical inferences, and still-open mechanisms for gravitational waves, dark matter, and dark energy.
lesson_media.caption: Modern cosmology has strong evidence for several phenomena while their deeper causes remain unknown; those are different levels of uncertainty.
